blocks.x: SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview of
Garvin Bushell
Interviewed by Monk Montgomery

Washington, D.C.
August, 1977

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS

My name is Monk Montgomery and I have the honor and the distinct pleasure to announce and interview, in my estimation, one of the most exciting and distinguished living legends of today, Mr. Garvin Bushell. And through the courtesy of the Smithsonian Institution I was asked to interview Garvin Bushell and I'm really happy to have the opportunity.

Garvin Bushell, as you may or may not know, is one of the most exciting musicians of our day and time and it stems back from the very beginning, the early days of jazz music. And I would like to introduce Garvin Bushell by asking him where was his home town and state?

(unintelligible) Monk. Originally I came out of Ohio, was born in Ohio -- Springfield, Ohio, to be exact. They have it stated that I was born in 1902, and in rummaging through some of the effects of my mother when she passed in '68, I found a book stating that I was born in 1900. So, give or take, it was either 1902 or 1900, anyhow, it was very close to the beginning of the 20th Century, in Springfield. As I recollect, there was a very happy atmosphere in Ohio in those days when I was a kid. Nothing but pleasure and a lot of good music, I remember distinctly. And as we grew up we began to hear some very good marching bands and it seems as though Springfield was sort of in tune with the progress of American popular music -- not only Springfield, but Columbus was also a
town that -- Columbus, Ohio?
Oh, yes, Columbus, Ohio. And then it extended over into Indianapolis.
Indiana.

Yes, Indiana. Yes, because I remember distinctly a lady came to Springfield -- her first name was Irene. A very fine pianist -- this was about 1910 or 11 and since then I've heard that she became the wife of Teddy Wilson, who taught Teddy Wilson how to play piano. She came out of Indiana, out of Indianapolis. And it seems as though ragtime was just the major thing to have for your parties and the new tunes as they came out -- Springfield had them. As soon as New York turned them loose, then they came to Springfield and Columbus. So, I find that a lot of jazz musicians and classical musicians came out of Ohio. The great Ted Lewis came out of Circleville.
Is that right?
Oh, yes, he was born in Ohio.
Circleville, Ohio.
Yes, yes. And there's another fine -- one of the first tenor players to record -- he came also out of Springfield, so --
Garvin, can I back up a little bit and ask you a couple of questions? For example, are you from a

Yes, yes, yes. I guess it was passed on. My mother was a vocal teacher and a fine singer, and my father was also a vocal teacher. And I had an uncle who played clarinet in the circus and, as I say, my family -- we didn't get a piano until about 1909, but before --

Yes, when I came on the scene we had an organ, one of those pedal things that you pedal, you know? And I had also an uncle who played piano and he would come over and play Scott Joplin on the organ, you know, -- or ragtime, it wasn't necessarily Scott Joplin, but in later years, say, in 1911 or 12, he was playing Maple Leaf Rag, I remember distinctly. Scott Joplin.
Let me ask you another question. Are there sisters and brothers that you have in your family?
I have a sister, but she never was interested in music. She lives in Denver now -- in the mid-west in Denver, Colorado.
Was she older or younger?
She's younger than I am.
Well, then when you got into music at the very beginning, do you recall what age it was when you were --

Well, I began piano when I was about ten years old and I studied piano for four years. One of my teachers was a descendent of the great Rafer Johnson, the decathlon winner from some years ago at Antioch Collech in Yellow Springs, Ohio. I remember he used to come up to the house -- come all the way from Yellow Springs, nine miles, to give me a piano lesson, and charge me 50 cents. And I remember he drive his first car up to the house. It was a Ford; he paid $550.00 for it. And he was elated, so he could hardly give me my lesson telling me about this new automobile.
What a thrill he had with his Ford.
Oh, yes, yes.
How often did you take a lesson from him at 50 cents a lesson?
Once a week.
Once a week. he'd drive over, huh?
Once a week, 50 cents a lesson. Oh, that was --
The price was right.
In those days, yes, yes. And he'd come to the house, you know. I didn't have to go to him, he'd come to the house.
What instrument was he teaching at the time?
Piano.
Piano.
Yes, piano. We finally got a piano --
You actually started with the piano.

Piano was my first instrument, yes. I find that now, having studied piano it gave me a foundation -- a harmonic foundation a lot of musicians just didn't have, and it gave me -- I became conscious of harmony along with the melody. I find so many musicians today -- they learn a melody but they never learn the harmonic construction. In those days, any time you learned a tune you learned the harmony the same time you learned the melody. Therefore, you can analyze.
Right.
And it made improvisation much easier.
I agree.
Surely.

Now, just coming up, if you can recall from -- that was during the period when you were about ten years old. Right? Now, can we go step-by-step as you grew into the other instruments -- the other musicians of that early period? Who you played with during that --

Well, I would like to give you a little story about our first job that I played. You know, we organized a band in Springfield and there were six of us. And we were all members of a club called the Douglas Debating Society and we had rehearsed until we got so we could play about four tunes.
So, when our club decided to give a dance at our dance hall in Springfield, why they wanted to hire the orchestra that was -- A sextet.

A sextet -- called a big orchestra in those days, six pieces. An orchestra that was affiliated with the club. So they decided to pay us a dollar and a half apiece for our job for that night. We played at the Oddfellow's Hall.
Was this a dance?

A dance, yes, a public dance. And the Douglas Debating Society's first dance. A new club, young club, youngsters, you know. And we played -- we played -- the people seemed to like it, but somehow or another the powers that be of the club didn't like what we played so at the next meeting they voted that we should give the dollar and a half back. That was my experience with my first job. I got paid then they took it away from me.
Right. Now, once you get paid, then you become professional. But they took the money back, so you're still an amateur.
They took the money back so I'm still an amateur.
You just also mentioned the fact that -- about relating to the sextet as an orchestra. They didn't use the phrase -- the meaning -- sextet didn't mean sextet then?
No, they didn't say sextet. It was just --
it was a band, it was a jazz band.
Well, how large a group would you have to have before you were regarded as a band?

Well, a band wasn't used in the terms of dance. Only with the circus bands. The local bands, the local groups or the local orchestras -- they were always called orchestras, even four pieces -- they called it an orchestra.
Is that right?

Yes. And a band was a big brass band which you found with the circus, usually about 15 or 18 pieces. I know when I played -- 1916 I went with the circus -- that's what they had, 18 pieces. But they called them an orchestra. For instance, our group was six pieces and it was actually the beginning, because the members of this group became later on McKinney's Cotton Pickers.
The members out of that six piece --

It originated in Springfield, Ohio -- McKinney's Cotton Pickers, because McKinney was a drummer in Springfield, and our original group composed of Lloyd Scott, Don Frye, Luther Watson, McKinney, and later on came Milt Senior, who was one of the first saxophonists in the State of Ohio -- and that was the beginning of the Cotton Pickers.
And all five out of the six went into the McKinney --
Yes -- became McKinney's Cotton -- and

Dave Wilburn -- I forgot -- on banjo -- Dave Wilburn. And Dave was with the Cotton Pickers for 30 years. I imagine that's the only orchestra he ever played with -- McKinney's Cotton Pickers. So they originated in Springfield, Ohio. But before even we organized our group there were groups like Willis and Warmack out of Dayton, Ohio; Brown from Columbus, Ohio; Don O'Niel from Springfield. These were four-piece, saxophone, piano -- no bass -- banjo and drums. Didn't use a bass then at all.
How did you -- how did the groups get around? You said that -- Ohio and Springfield --
In cars and -- in automobiles, surely.
They would travel down to Springfield.

Yes, they'd travel, surely. They traveled. Then we had the electric cars between Springfield, Columbus, Cincinnati and Dayton. One car propelled -- they called them traction cars. But most of the bands would buy an old jalopy and -- a couple of them and carried them around in their own car. And one car would hold -- as I say, there was only about four pieces, but if you had drums to bring along and music, they'd maybe do it in two cars. But these bands traveled all over Ohio and Indiana and even as far east as Pittsburgh. Yeah. Columbus was very smart on jazz in those days -- it was sharp.
Well, how long did the sextet stay together?
Well, I left -- the summer of '16 I went

with the circus and I did a season with the circus sitting beside my uncle. He played E-flat clarinet and I played B flat clarinet. Incidentally, we didn't bring in the time that I started studying clarinet. Four years of piano and then I had -- from 14 on I started studying clarinet.
I see.

By myself, teaching myself. The only lessons I had were when my uncle would come in off of the circus and show me where to put this finger and that finger and I already had some knowledge of music, and -- well, I could sing better music than I could play it because I was taught solfeggio from the very beginning, first grade in Ohio. They teach you sight singing. They taught it in those days from the very first grade.
In grade school.
In grade school, the very first year in school you were taught do, re, me, fa, sol, la, ti, do, and the pitch and the value. To this day I can look at a note now and know the pitch before I play it.
That's interesting.

And I never had a lesson in solfeggio only what we would have in grade schools. And it held up. I went to conservatory in Puerto Rico about ten years ago and I had to have solfeggio on my studies, and I could do it better than the students that had been there for years, studying

two or three years. I had it since grade school. So they use immovable do -- that system is with the C it's called do -- I don't care what key you're in -- if it's in the key of F, C is called do. But in our system, if you're in the key of F, do would be fa, you see. That's the rule. That's the system used.
I understand.
So, I had that beginning. So, I went to the circus in 1916 I did a season sitting beside my uncle.

Can I ask you a question here in regards to the circus? You said you went with the circus -- does that mean you would travel with the circus or you played only with the circus only when it was in town?

Yes, when the circus was playing. Well, that was -- we were the side-show band. I went on the road with them in the side-show band, and I stayed, I think, two months because it was too much for me and -- well, naturally, my vacation was over. It was more of an experience my uncle wanted me to get.
It was just during the summer when you were out of school that you traveled with them.
Yeah, and we had 18 pieces -- 16 pieces -- it was $18.00 a week. That's where the 18 comes in. $18.00 a week.
In a circus band?
Sixteen pieces and we had -- we got $18.00 a week, room and board -- naturally, you lived on the car and they fed you -- the circus.
I see. Well, how did you perform?
Like -- Well, you know how the side shows --
Big shows or just the side shows?

Side show. You know, they'd have -- they didn't have any black bands in the big tops in those days. Only in the side show, and then we had a minstrel show. They called them beck and wing dancing and singers and blues, and when the "Memphis Blues" came out I remember -- "Beale Street Blues" and various sorts of blues and ragtime. We played "Maple Leaf," we played "Entertainer" -- the very "Entertainer" that was just recently popular in the picture The Entertainer. [The Sting]
Yeah.
Incidentally, I brought a recording of that that I made with Bunk? I brought that along today.
Well, we'll play some after a bit.
Yeah.

I'm still interested about your doing the area of the circus days and the carnival -- or the side shows and that type thing. Did you involve yourself beyond playing? Were you -- did you do singing or dancing or --
No, no, I didn't, I was just a boy and
scared to death and stayed right under my uncle's coat tail. In those days every performer -- the circus had a .45 in his pocket.
A gun, you mean, a .45.
Oh, my goodness, yes. And they were rough and tough people.
Was there a reason for that?
My mother had enough of that. Two months of that, you know.
Well, did you have to audition for the job or they just brought you along and --
No, my uncle said that my nephew can do the job and they -- you know, take him for experience. And they me $18.00 for my -- every week.
Obviously they were satisfied with your playing.

Well, I just -- just because my uncle -- he played a very difficult instrument -- E flat clarinet was one of the hardest instrument in the band and he was important, so they took his word for it. And, I wasn't playing too much, you can be sure of that -- I wasn't playing too much. I was hitting one note out of four, you know.
But it was a great experience.
Terrific experience. It gave me an insight on people that I didn't know. I used to watch them

every night and look at the faces of various people and types and their reaction. And traveling in the show with show people I learned a lot of things I shouldn't have learned inthose days, but it gave me an early start on experience.
Yeah. Well, from the circus you veered out to bigger and better things.

Well, yes. I came back and they decided then that I should go to -- I got through my high school. I went to Pittsburgh to high school and I came back from there and I went to Wilberforce University. And I met a lot of guys there and I was also in the band there and met the great Claude Jones who became one of the country's great trombone players, Claude Jones. And I met Edgar Hayes who's now in Los Angeles, a tremendous pianist.
Was in the university or in high school.

No, no this was university. Wilberforce University is now Central State. And incidentally, in the circus I learned about the origin of the word jazz. It was just becoming popular then and I thought I ought to mention that because I've had many people come to me and ask where did the word originate -- jazz. I'm quite sure it originated in Louisiana. In New Orleans in those days the perfume was a very big industry, you know, the French brought it over with them, and they used jasmine -- the oil of jasmine -- to insert
in all different odors to pep it up. It gave it -- it made the odor -- it gave more force to it, you might say. And if a perfume was dead, they put a little jasmine oil in there, mix it in --
Jasmine was an oil.

Yeah, from the oil of jasmine, from the flower, I guess, the jasmine. And that seemed to pep up most perfumes, give the scent more force to it. Anyhow, so they'd say, well, let's jazz it up a bit, it's a little dead. Jazz it up a bit. And out of that they said, when you started improvising, they said, well, jazz it up a bit, you know, give your own concept of the melody. Give the melody more force, more presence of the melody. So, it came about that if you improvised on the original of a melody of a composer, they said, well, you're jazzing it up. You play it straight and they'd say, now jazz it up. And you'd improvise. So, it went on even to the famous red light district of New Orleans. They began to use the same word.
It kind of caught on.
Yes, it caught on and they used it in the place of jazz. A woman would approach you and --'Is jazz in your mind tonight, young fellow?'
But that jazz it was taken from, the word itself --
Jasmine.
Jasmine, was spelled with a j-a-s-s-
J-a-s-s-.
Yes.

I think Earl Fuller, to my knowledge, made one of the first recordings using -- he said -- he had j-a-z-z or j-a-s-s -- the Dixieland Jazz Band used j-a-s-s- I think. The j-a-z-z came later, but it was originally j-a-s-s. Yeah.
Well, that's great. Well, after your school days of the university, then you -- were you still in your home town -- went back to your home town of Springfield?

No, I'll tell you what happened in that case. While going to school I wanted a clarinet -- a new clarinet. The one I had wasn't adequate. And they were -- all the guys were wearing Cordovan shoes in those days and I just spent my allowance and I wanted a pair of Cordovan shoes and a new clarinet. So, one of my roommates lived in Dayton, Ohio. I said, "If I had an extra job, I could buy a clarinet and shoes." He said, "Well, why don't you go over to Dayton and get a job." So, I said, "Cut class?" and he said, "Yeah, cut class. You want a clarinet and you want new shoes." He said, "It won't cost nothing, you can live at my house." So, sure enough I went to Dayton with him on the weekend and I went out that Monday morning -- he cut class for a few days -- we left

Wilberforce, which is 24 miles -- or more than that -- 24 miles from Wilberforce, Dayton is, and I got a job at the National Cash Register. And -- pouring -- skimming the slag off of hot brass as they poured it in the molds to make these cash registers.
This is like in a foundry?

Yeah, in a foundry, the foundry section. And, incidentally, I had to walk two and a half miles to work right along the banks of the Miami River, and I remember distinctly it was two and three below zero all that time. And I'd walk that at 5:00 o'clock in the morning and hit those two miles and be there at 6:30 in the morning to start work -- working at that foundry. I worked two weeks, got my pay, and decided to come back -- to go back to school, back to Wilberforce. So, the day that I arrived back at Wilberforce I saw this huge man standing on the stoop of O'Niel hall. I said, "That's looks familiar." He turned around and it really was, it was my father. He weighed 217, big guy. He didn't speak to me. He said, "Son, go upstairs and pack your clothes." I said, "What --" "No, no, no questions, go upstairs and pack your clothes." The school had notified him in New York -- they were living in New York then, my mother and father. And, incidentally, I'd been living all those years, most of my life, with my grandmother. My father and mother were teaching school in Texas.
I see.
Yes. And, so, he said, "Go upstairs and pack your clothes." So, I packed my clothes and the next morning I was on a train coming to New York. That was 1919 -- that's how I happened to be in New York.
Did you get the shoes?

I got the shoes and my clarinet. Oh, yes. I got my shoes and clarinet. Yes, yes. The guy tried to keep me -- I remember a guy named Bob White -- he was a pianist -- tried his best to get me to stay in Dayton. I said, "No, I've got to get back to school. It's important. I've got to go back to school." And that's how I come to New York. Otherwise, I'd still been in Ohio probably -- had I not gone to Dayton and cut class and they notified my parents and they got on a train and came right out to Ohio after.
So, this was about 1919 that you actually moved to New York.
1919. Yeah. They brought me to New York. The latter part of 1919.
Right. Well, did you, at that time, in moving to New York, you had completed -- did that finish your university --
No, I didn't finish. No, I was only my second year, second year. At Wilberforce.
But after you got to New York --
I never went back to school.
You didn't go back to school?

No, I didn't go back to school. I decided I wanted to play clarinet and it broke my father's heart. You know, he just couldn't see it, me being a musician and all that he could see in being a musician was playing the circus -- like my uncle was. And I stuck with it and I wasn't very good either. To be frank with you -- I didn't read well, I didn't play well, but I was learning. I had the ambition -- I wanted to be -- and that's the big thing in learning. As long as the youngster has that desire to become -- he'll make it his business to get on the right track.
Yeah, I agree with you there.

And I state that to my students all the time. First of all you must have the desire to learn. Without that I don't care what sort of teacher you have or what kind of natural talent you have -- you'll only go so far. But that desire has to be there always, even to this day, I still have a desire to be one of the finest oboe players in the world. I'll never be, but I believe so -- I think I will.
That's beautiful.
I get up every day with that in mind.
That's beautiful. I totally agree with you. What took place after you got to New York -- with your music?
Well, my first recollection of contact

with musicians was a fellow by the name of Clarence Potter. He heard about this clarinet player from Ohio -- it was a big joke -- This Clarence Potter was a very dark Negro who had sharp, sharp features and he did Scottish imitations. He imitated Sir Harry Lauder. He sang in Scotch, he did the number, he wore kilts, and did everything like Harry Lauder. Clarence Potter.
He was strictly a singer?

A singer, singer, yeah. He sang songs just like Harry Lauder sings, in Scotch, and he was real dark but he had real sharp features. Looked as though -- like some other race, blacked up -- that's the way he looked. Very handsome guy, short and stocky. So we rehearsed for about three or four weeks and had this act. He had been an entertainer around New York, you know. In those days entertaining, singing musicians were the thing. You know, if you couldn't sing, you didn't make the money. It wasn't so much dance as it was entertainment. And we had an act formed -- Clarence Potter and his Jazz Babies.
Jazz babies?

Yes. So, we had a Sunday concert -- they called them concerts because at the burlesque houses they didn't work burlesque on Sunday, so they had vaudeville on Sundays. So we did this Sunday concert at the Lyric's Lyric in Hoboken, New Jersey -- last town in the world -- Hoboken. Well, let me tell you, the act was so bad, after the first show the manager came
back and gave us two dollars and a half for our transportation back to Manhattan.
Two dollars and a half --
Two dollars --
How large was that group?
Well, we had a five-piece band and a singer.
Five-piece band.
Five-piece band and a singer.
Uh-huh.

That was my first trip on -- actually on the stage outside of the circus, with a platform, more or less. And, then I met -- they said for me to come rehearse with another group called Daisey Martin and her Jazz Bellhops.
These names.
Yes. And --
Well, how did they get Jazz Bellhops? Were they actually bellhops, or --
No, no. We had bellhop uniforms on, you know, the red --
Oh, I see.
Remember Johnny for Phillip Morris? The uniform --
Yes.
Same only red. And we made about four records on OKeh.
What year was this?

This must have been 1920. 1920. Because Mamie Smith had made her "Right Here for You" and "Crazy Blues" -- I didn't make that with Mamie. A "Good Man is Hard to Find" -- yeah. I made "Right Here for You" and "Crazy Blues", but she had already had two sides out in 1920, being the first Negro woman to sing on record -- the first blues --
I see. Can you tell us a little about -- what was recording like during the period of your first recording with the Bellhops?
Oh, yes.
What was recording like?
It was an experience.
In the studio.

Compared to today's recording, it was like the difference between hitching a horse to a rig and having a Cadillac car. It was just that far apart. No, we have to -- you go to a studio -- we recorded for Okeh which was on 45th Street in New York. You sat on high stools, each horn player, and you had a long tube that extended out from the control room with a bell on the end, like an old-time gramophone but the bell wasn't quite as large, but extended through a long pipe, and it had the flare on the end -- you played into the pipe. There were no such things as microphones then.
With five musicians, does that mean
there were five pipes or did all five of you play through one pipe?

Yes, there was one -- the piano was picked up by an overall pipe, but the trumpet was picked up by one pipe and the trumbone from another and the clarinet from another. And there were no drums, naturally, used -- nor bass.
There was no drums or bass--
No drums or bass.
-- recorded at that time. Was there a reason?

Well, of course, it recorded into a plate of bees wax and I understand that if either one of those instruments would make such large indentations in the wax and would make a bump and it couldn't take it.
You couldn't use -- did that go for a snare drum, as well?
Share drum as well. They -- later on they began to use wood block and share drum, but never a bass drum.
Never a bass.

Until they finally got so that they called it orthophonic -- they began to put orthophonic recording then they could -- that came out in the late '20's. And then they could use the bass and -- well, in '25 they used bass in Germany. But, that's the way those vocal records were made then
with no drums and no bass. But there was no electricity involved at all. We even had to crank up the turn table.
Is that right?
Yes, yes. There was no electricity involved at all. No microphones. I hadn't even heard of a microphone.
You mean they'd crank up the turn table in the studio?

They cranked it up -- it had a spring -- yes, in the studio, back in the control room. Yes. They didn't have it run by motor. They cranked it up -- wound it up just like you did a player. Even our phonographs had to be cranked up. There was no motor. That didn't come about until later on. And, you had -- you only made two numbers in a whole session and you didn't get paid by the time, you got paid by the amount of numbers that you made. And it would take you all day to do two numbers.
Why so?

Because of the playbacks and the blending. They couldn't blend, there was no way to blend, they -- just by moving the guy back, turn this way a little more, turn that way a little more, and, as I say, electronics weren't involved, so they had no way to control it, see.
I see.
Either move you away or pull you forward
or move you back.
I see.
And it would take us all day to do two numbers. No such thing as doing an album. They never heard of that.
Well, was it legal in the way of being legal for recording at that time -- did you have to go through the contracts and all that business?
No, no. As a matter of fact, in New York then there was no such -- 802 was just young and 21 -- in 1920 there wasn't any 802, there was 308 or 310 or something like that.
That was a white local?
Yeah, it was a white local. None of us -- none of the Negro musicians belonged to that.
The Blacks couldn't join the local?
So we freelanced. And when we became a threat and an opposition, then 802 was formed and they made us join.
Yeah.
However, we could play where we wanted -- theaters, plenty of places. We had no union protection and we could play where we wanted to and --
How did you arrive at prices? How were they fixed for the Blacks?
Well, they just fixed -- $30.00 a record. And you played two sides. You got $30.00 for it. If it took you six hours it was $30.00. If it took you two hours it was $30.00. That was the price.
I see.
But, I'll tell you, the fellow that wrote 'Crazy Blues' and 'Right Here for You' -- a controller name of Smith -- he made $90,000 on his first check from Okeh, and --
Of royalties?
Of royalties. $90,000 -- and $90,000 in those days was worth quarter of a million now, I think.
Exactly, exactly.
Peery Bradford -- he was the guy that did it.
What did records sell for in those days out of the stores?
Seventy-five cents.
It was like our records? Two sides?

It was just a record, two sides. Seventy-five cents. Yeah. Speaking about recording, the next session I did was with Mamie Smith and the way Peery Bradford heard me -- he was her manager then and also the writer of those tunes -- I lived at 130th Street and Peery lived directly behind me on 129th Street and he had heard me practicing on my house and he said, 'Hey, clarinet player,' I didn't know him, he didn't know

me. He said, "You play clarinet, huh?" I said, "Yeah, I try to." "How'd you like to make some records?" I said, "Fine." "Come on over my house," so I strapped my clarinet case on my back and climbed over the back fence and went through his kitchen upstairs and there was Mamie Smith sitting there.
That's when you met Mamie Smith.
That's when I -- yeah. Mamie Smith -- and from then on I have recorded, and after making records with her the following summer I went on the road with her.
How large was that group?
That was five-piece -- five-piece band. Trumpet, trombone, clarinet, piano, drums.
This was still in New York City?

Originated in New York City, yes. I'll tell you, Johnny Dunn, the famous Johnny Dunn had quit so we hired Bubber Miley. I guess -- you know, he became very famous with Duke Ellington, and he had never been on stage before. And we opened in Pittsburgh, and Mamie had all new costumes made, and those days singers wore big feathers and plumes and there were no zippers -- it was all hook and eyes, you know.
Yeah.

And Mamie had this new costume, gorgeous costumes made so the opening day in Pittsburgh, at the Pershing Theater we played our first tune, 'Royal Garden Blues.' Bam -- played a 'vamp' big hand. All right. Now, we (unintelligible) right here for

you, if you don't get it, it ain't no fault of -- then the introduction bringing her on. No Mamie. So, her husband said, "Play the introduction again." We played it again, dah, dah, dah, dah. No Mamie. So he said, "Play the Royal Garden Blues again." Well, now, Bubber's scared to death. It's his first day on stage -- first time ever on stage, and his lip is giving out, so he played the Royal Garden Blues through and through, completely again, and the people applaud and say, "Hey, you played it once." So he said, "Play the introduction." Mamie's downstairs -- we don't know -- she's struggling with her costume. She's hooked up in the -- on the corner of her dresser and can't get it loose out of her dresser drawer -- and, I don't know -- everything happened. She couldn't get her dress on. Half on and half off. So, Bubber got excited and we played the introduction again and oh she said, "Play it again." By that time Bubber's frightened. I looked over there at Bubber and he was so nervous he had his trumpet down on his chin trying to blow it. And he's backing off of the stage at the same time. Backing up all at the same time and he's trying to find his mouth, scared to death. And her husband -- out to the wing, with Bubber backed off in the wing, and literally took his foot and booted him back on the stage, and the audience yelled. They had to bring the curtain down. Now, that was our first show in Pittsburgh.
Did it look like a great act?
Oh, it was a great act. The people screamed.
Let me ask a little bit about Mamie in terms of what was her personality like as a person?

Mamie, in my mind, was what we called a shouter. She wasn't a blues singer like Bessie. Bessie was truly a blues singer. But Mamie was the first to record and naturally she would be the first one considered. She was a very fine looking woman, nice personality, easily led. She usually had a husband that was a big bruiser, one of those kinds of things, taking all of her money. She finally got another husband by the name of Goldberg and he interfered with the money -- something like that -- I left her then. Anyhow, on that tour on the road we played Kansas City, 12th Street Theater. So we had acts with us -- we engaged other acts. So we had to enlarge our band. We put on a saxophone and a bass and a violin -- we got a violin out of Detroit. And this saxophone player came in -- this young fellow with the saxophone -- never heard of him before, sat down in the pit, played -- played every part, didn't miss a note. Told him to take a solo. He took a tremendous solo. We said, 'What is your name?' He said, 'Coleman.' 'Coleman who?' 'Coleman Hawkins.'
Is that right?
'How old are you?' 'Fifteen.' He was fifteen years old.
What year was this?
It was '21.
He was 15 years old in 1921. A lot of people thought Coleman was much older. He was 15 years old in 1921.
Well, he's 15 -- that was perhaps one of his --
Hum?
At the age of 15, it was perhaps one of his first jobs to go out on.
Well, the young fellow had such a vast knowledge of music and jazz it could hardly have been his first job. He must have played someplace before.
I mean, to go on the road to travel, I mean, he wouldn't travel any younger than that.

Well, no, he didn't travel with us then because the reason why, we wanted to take him. He went to St. Joe to play -- that's his home, St, Joe, Missouri, and I asked his grandmother, I said, 'We like him so much and he's a great artist and we want him to go with us.' She said, 'Well, no, he's just a baby, he's only 15 years old.'
But he didn't look it.
No, he -- well, then he looked young. He was a handsome kid. He looked young, very young. And she didn't

let him go. So I didn't go with them the next season. The following season they went back out there -- what it was, there was girl that had taken a liking to Coleman and his grandmother didn't like her family, so she let him join the band the next season to get him our of St. Joe, so he -- and that's how he came to New York. That's how Coleman got to New York. I told Frieda, his sister (unintelligible), does he really play? Well, he's tremendous.
I'm sure he had no trouble when he got to New York.

Oh, he got a job, he worked at a place called the Garden of Joy, a big Rock (unintelligible) from there on he joined Fletcher -- went down to the -- not the Bamboo Inn, another place on 129th Street. That's where Fletcher heard him. Yeah, he's a great artist. Been nothing like him anyplace on any instrument. He's like Louis, he hit the scene just like Louis did and exploded on the scene. Nobody ever played jazz on any instrument like Coleman. No, I think -- I played with him for five years later on with Fletcher's and I never heard him hit a bad note -- never. Never did I hear -- brand new arrangements, I don't care what the key or the signature was, I never heard Coleman make a bad note.
That's remarkable.
Never in five years.
But New York -- actually you made
New York your home over a period of many years.
I would say 50. About 50 years were my headquarters there. You know, back and forth to Europe or Africa, but New York was home.
After leaving Mamie, did you go back to --
No, I went back to the cabaret after I left Mamie. Back into the cabarets and Leroy's.
Was this in New York?
Yeah, yeah. 135th and Fifth Avenue -- one of the most sensational joints I've ever been in in my life. There was a shooting -- at least three a week and a murder once a month.
In the cabaret?
Oh, yes, Leroy's. And there was a black cabaret that absolutely did not allow white people in -- they wouldn't let them come under no circumstances. Ted Lewis was the only man --
Where was it located again?

135th Street and Fifth Avenue, down in the cellar. I remember one night they beat up on a fellow and they put him out. He shot the doorman upstairs, he came down the stairs and stood at the foot of the stairs and just starts shooting across the cabaret. Well, our piano set back in a little alcove like, and we had six in the band -- we had a tuba, then --

incidentally, these were Jenkins boys that worked in this cabaret, all from Jenkins Orphanage. In those days the best brass men in the country, Jabbo Smith, Gus Akins, and those guys came out of Fred Cooley, clarinet player, [unintelligible] came out of [Kewley] L.A. Jenkins Orphanage from South Carolina. That band traveled all over the world and played on street corners for collection, that's how they kept the school going -- it was an orphanage school. And except Willy Gant the rest of us were geechees out of South Carolina and from Jenkins Orphanage and Willy Gant and myself. So, this guy shot and I remember hearing those bullets buzz, buzz, past the bandstand. Well, now, the piano was back in an alcove and after the third shot was fired I think they pulled out the piano and all six of us got behind the piano. Everybody dove behind this piano -- all six men behind the piano. You know somebody had to be on the bottom, and one of those was me, because I was little and I scooted and after that first shot I made my CURVE and was behind -- Willy Gant pulled the piano out, he was the piano player, and right under, back behind the piano there were the other five right on top.
Well, how did you manage -- the group manage to consistently work -- is this something you get used to or --
Yes, you get used to that because of the elements.
This is the thing that happens in cabarets?

Yes, the element -- you get used to it. In all the cabarets in Harlem there was always a big fight in those days because the kind -- it was during Prohibition naturally, the '20's, and the stuff that they were drinking, it just -- the people had no control, they just went wild and they'd fight and shoot and cut and break up the place, and we were used to it. And every cabaret had three or four bouncers in it -- you know, they had to have. We were on Lenox Avenue, and they had some of the toughest guys in Harlem as bouncers. And we got used to it. But the first few months my experience was, I would come home nervous wreck. You played til 5:00, 6:00 o'clock in the morning, you know. That's no lie, you played until the people left. No such time limit as you played four hours or six hours. You started at 9:00 and you played.
You just started at a certain time.

Yeah, you played. At 6:00 o'clock you'd say, "Okay, that's enough." Maybe, if it's 6:30, "Oh, you can cut it now." But you played, and you got $35.00 a week in tips. $35.00 a week in tips. And me -- it was a great experience. It taught me how to play in all keys. It taught me songs, it gave me a chance -- because an entertainer went around to every table and she sang at least 15 or 18 choruses before she'd finish. She thought she had enough money and she
had a whole fist full of dollars and some down her stockings, the side of some in her girdle and --
Then you actually made pretty good in tips.

Well, yes, it had to go, say, six, about ten ways -- I'd make $5.00, $6.00 maybe a night, something like that, plus -- oh, yeah, I saved quite a bit, saved quite a bit as a youngster then. Then (while in unintelligible) Leroy's -- there was an act out on the road called The Modern Cocktail and [Pantages] it went into vaudeville then with this act on Plantageous circuit all the way to the coast and back. It was a jazz band, five-piece jazz band, singer and dancer.
And that was consistent traveling?
Yeah, every week.
Were they locations or one-nighters?

No, no, vaudeville, vaudeville. If you -- you either did a full week or a split week. We called a split week -- three days in this town, four days in the other. There's no day off, you know, in vaudeville. If you worked a week in a theater you did seven days. So that was -- well, we did the Pantages, we picked it up in Chicago and went all the way out to Seattle and on down towards --
Did you travel with the whole show or --
No, no, just our pack. We were one time with the great Burns of Burns and Allen. He was the act ahead of
us when we did the lower circuit. He had a partner, he was a straight man and his partner was a comedian. George Burns. We traveled with him --
George Burns, Gracie Allen.
Yeah, yeah, George Burns. And one of those guys who did Tobacco Road -- we did the tour with him once.
Well, how did you travel at that time, by car, by train?

By train, yes. You got your ticket in Chicago and set up, sometimes, it was an overnight jump, you had a Pullman. You had to Pullman out of your -- or they had to pay half of it. You paid half or you could sit up all night. You'd pay half of your pullman berth.

At that time, during that period, a group such as that particular group -- were they considered or regarded a well-known group through, like, well, not -- I don't mean -- so far as they were promoted, heavily promoted through radio --

No, there was no radio -- no, no, radio didn't come about until '23, you know, became popular in '23 -- latter part of '22, into '23. No, it was vaudeville and it was advertised at the theaters themselves or in the local newspapers, vaudeville was, but not -- it didn't have to be a record group. You got a name as a vaudeville act. We also had another act Liza and her Shuffling Sextet. I'll get to that later because
it will involve Duke Ellington, see.
Yeah, I understand.
But, Vaudeville, you know, up on your marquee you had the name of the act -- we were the headliner act.
But I mean, if you come to a town for the first time, you know, well, people would -- they would actually go because it was just a vaudeville show, or --

Vaudeville show, they usually had six or eight acts and they went just as a habit. In most communities people go to see the show, maybe twice a week. If it's a split-week town, and they have different acts -- one act for -- one set of acts for three days and another set for the last half of the week which lasts four days, they'd go to the theater twice a week. But they always went to the vaudeville house. They didn't know what they were going to see. Unless there was a headline that they knew about.
Yeah, such as George and --
Of course, our act, Modern Cocktail -- that was their second time around so they had a reputation in vaudeville.
I see.
And I was getting the enormous sum of $75.00 a week.
Were your expenses paid? Or did you
have to pay your own expenses out of that?
Well, you could get a meal for 50 cents. Sunday dinner, 75 cents. A dollar a night for your room.
Your transportation, what about that?
No, they paid transportation.
They paid for transportation.
Oh, sure, sure, transportation. All you paid was your hotel and your food.
You paid your hotel and food.

You could live on $2.00 a day easily. And then have some change left. $2.00 a day and you were living fine -- a dollar a day for your room at the hotel and, say, 50 cents for breakfast and 65 cents for dinner. Sunday it was a dime more, 75.
How long -- you were on the road with that group. How long did you travel with them from the west coast to New York?

Oh, I stayed with that group until -- one trip. Then we came back and we organized this group of our own -- Liza and her Shuffling Sextet. That was the group -- Fats Waller was the pianist, Clarence Robinson was the dancer, Katie Crippen was the singer, I played clarinet, and then we had a trumpet player and a trombone player whom I've forgotten.
Fats Waller was in this group --
Oh, yeah, he was the pianist.
Liza and her Shuffling Sextet.

Yeah. Now, Robinson and I -- we were in partnership owning the act. We owned the act, Clarence Robinson and myself. And we got to Washington and Clarence said -- something went wrong. Clarence and I got in a terrific argument. And so we decided to split up, but before that happened, we heard this band play in a place in Washington called the Grapevine -- five-piece band, a banjo, drums, piano, trumpet and saxophone, five pieces.
Was this in Washington, D.C.?

Washington, D.C. So, Clarence came back and said, 'I heard a group last night that was terrific.' So I went down to hear them and sure enough there was this group, and the group was headed by Elmer Snowden, he was a banjo player, and in the band was a youngster playing piano, and his name was Duke Ellington. They always nicknamed him Duke because of his heir, with Edward Kennedy.
Yeah.

And Toby Hardwick on saxophone and the Sheet, trumpet. Sonny Greer playing drums. So Clarence and I had this big argument and said we'll break up. Clarence had this in mind anyhow. He saw an opportunity. So, he went to Showden and said, 'I've got a job for you.' In the meantime we'd had the entire Polley circuit booked which is six and a half weeks with the act. Now, when we broke up and Clarence

said, 'Go ahead, I got a group. I can take -- I got a group, I'll take over that (unintelligible).' So I said we'll beat him to it. So I got into New York early Monday morning and I went down to the Palace Theater office and told them that Clarence was bringing in a brand new act. I had the original band, which I did have -- the band went with me. I had the original band and he's bringing a brand new band. So, immediately they cancelled the [Polley] Time and Clarence had brought this band to New York, Duke and Showden and that bunch, and they had to split hot dogs for weeks around New York, because I cancelled the work -- I cancelled all the work.
Is that right?

Yes. And I told them about (unintelligible). 'Good, you get them, you get them.' So he said, 'All right.' So he brought Snowden and his band to New York thinking that he was going to have the [Polley] Time but I beat him to the punch and I got there before and cancelled it all. Now, Fats stayed with me, Fats and Katie and all. So we went on, we got another dancer and still Liza and her Shuffling Sextet.
Now tell me about Liza, all this is so interesting, I want to pull out some of these things. Liza was like -- what was she -- a singer, right?
She was a singer, Katie Crippen. She was our singer, blues singer, and we hired --
She was the leader, she -- this was her band.
No, it wasn't her band, no, no, no. We called it as an act, Liza and her Shuffling Sextet.
I see.

But we had hired her to sing, but you have to have a feature attraction in a vaudeville act. You have a center. The act was built around her, you see, and -- as a singer, and she did a little dance and she was the glamour of the act, you see. Five big rough men in tuxedos and all, but she was the glamour, nice looking girl. So you had an act like that you always -- the woman singer, you say, so and so and her jazzband. Mamie Smith and her Jazz -- Edith Wilson and her Jazz Hounds --
I see, but the band was like -- the band itself --

It was my band, my group. And Fats Waller, God bless him -- we used to have so much fun with him. Fats would come to the theater -- he always bought apples on a stick, you know, then he would get around 270, 285 pounds. He'd come down the street, wabbling down the street with one of these apples on a stick and every time we'd have to go we'd have to hide him because the law was always after him for non-payment of alimony, you know.
Oh he had too (unintelligible)
Oh, yes, she was -- every town we hit, "Fats?" No, he's not here -- we'd have to hide him first couple days. Sometimes we'd have to hire a pianist to play the first day.

Well, the world knows Fats Waller and is familiar with him and his music, but I would like to ask a little about Fats in terms of his personality and how he fit in with his music, what type of guy he was.
Yes, one of the all-time greats.
He always seemed so happy, jolly.

Yes, he was, he was. Let me tell you about Fats. A lot of the tunes in those days that the famous composers had their names on, Fats Waller wrote and he'd sell them for $50.00 and $25.00 and $30.00. I don't want to call the names of some guys that I know that bought his tunes that they gave him $50.00 for. Some of the tunes that he wrote.
And they turned out to be very --
Hits, yes, yes. But then he began to write tunes that were of his origin and his own name. But Fats--
How long was he with you?

I was with -- yes. We were in Boston on a New Year's night -- New Year's Eve -- we'd been out of New York then about two months, on the road, and we're lonesome. If you've ever had experience in Boston, you know what a town it was in those days -- might have been from what it is now -- New

Year's and the whistles are blowing and the bells are ringing and here we're sitting in this dingy Back Bay front room of this brown front and Fats has got a piano. He say, "Maccey I'd like to be in New York, wouldn't you?" "I certainly would love to be in New York." He goes, "blim, blim, blue, bue," you know, "Squeeze Me?" "blim, blee, blum," that tune he wrote in New Year's Eve and we were sitting there wishing we were in New York. He wrote that tune right then and there.
Is that right? Now, what year are we talking about?
That's 192 -- later part of '22 or the first part of '23. The first part of '23, yeah.
He was still working with you?
Yeah, yeah.
Did you have a co-leader or was it just you?

No, I was the leader of the band. And Fats was just a pianist, you know, he wasn't responsible. And he'd been playing organ at the Lincoln Theater and taking part in the cutting sessions they used to have down at Leroy's between Willie "The Lion" and James P.
Yeah, I heard --
And Freddy Tousell and Willy Gant and Fats. Fats was a youngster but he could still stride, but he was no match for James P. and Willie "The Lion". They'd

meet down at Leroy's, say on a Saturday night and it would last three and four hours, and it always ended up with James P. on top but Willie "The Lion" it was a toss-up, but James P. had a little more knowledge. But they were sensational -- to hear those guys play.
When they had those meets for those sessions I've heard talk of them, was it something that was sort of set up?

No, they were not set up. It was extemporaneous. They just -- you know, they'd wander out. A guy would go around a cabaret as they did back in the Teens -- you'd go around looking for somebody if you thought you could play, you'd go around looking for somebody to cut. When I say cut I mean out playing, you see.
Right.
And they call them cutting sessions, and that's where they got their experience. If you got cut then you learned from the other guy that cut you, see?
I see.
So that's the way they learned, and it was competitive, rag time piano was competitive.
But it was done in good sport.
Oh, yes, done in good sport, oh yes. I've never seen anything develop from that in the violent manner of any kind, unless with the spectators. But the musicians

themselves like Freddy Tonsell -- they'd meet and they'd go up to the Capital Palace. Willie "The Lion" was playing there and they'd go in and choose him and say, "Get up." And he'd play his ten choruses and then James P. would slide in and he'd play ten choruses and they go around and maybe the three of them would go around together, James P. and Fats and Aba Laba --
Aba Laba?
Aba Laba, yes. He was actually the creator of a lot of that style of shout piano, they called it --
They called it shout piano?
Shout piano, yes, yes. But Duke -- James was a big influence because he made QRS rolls, you know the piano rolls. He put all the "Carolina Shout" and those things on piano rolls.
Did Duke participate in those --

no, well, Duke went back to Washington. The strain was too much for Duke. Duke went back to Washington. Then he came back again and the band came back again and they got a job at 101 49th Street, down in the cellar, a place called Kentucky Club. The first time they didn't make it because they almost starved to death. They were splitting hot dogs and splitting malted milks. Duke went home and -- it was still Snowden's band -- Duke was just a piano player in the band.
Well, how did that come out --

All right. Now, they had a job at the Kentucky Club and Sonny -- to this day, you know, Sonny Greer -- well, Duke took care of Sonny, (41) [Duke] the day he died. He paid him $100.00 a week. He fired him out of the band because Sonny was (unintelligible) liquor head he fired him out of the band, but he paid him $100.00 a week for the rest of his life. Sonny conspired to get everybody to quit the band, quit Snowden and brought them back the next night as Duke Ellington's band. You see, Snowden quit -- they all quit Snowden, left him -- Snowden had no band, they quit, but they came back the next night with another banjo player and turned the band over to Duke.
Sonny Greer planned it that way.

Sonny planned it. Sonny did the whole maneuver, because he loved Duke. Ever since they were kids (unintelligible) And Duke took care of Sonny the rest of his days. The day he died he was getting $100.00 a week. Didn't have to work.
Well, it was no doubt --

He fired him because Sonny was a liquor head, he couldn't keep him in the band, and he wasn't playing the kind of drums that Duke needed, but he wasn't going to see Sonny go without because Sonny was the reason for him being.
I see. Without a doubt Duke was definitely a leader (unintelligible) himself out over the years.
Yes, yes. Duke --
How large was the band at that time?

Five pieces when they were at the Kentucky Club. Yes, five pieces. Then they added on a trombone player name of Charlie Irvis who did the plunger bit, the Tricky Sam, he created that. There was a fellow came from St. Louis did the wah-wah, the first one we heard do the plunger bit that Johnny Dunn had created back in 1920, and then invented the plunger. A fellow by the name of Jonas Walker came from St. Louis to New York and the trombone players heard him, so Charlie Irvis got some part of a little tin mute he used to use and did that growling, so he was the first trombone player with Duke before Tricky Sam, and -- but that's how the growl came about, Charlie Irvis. He was a New York kid too. And Bubber Miley was the other -- when they put the second trumpet on they put Bubber Miley in there, and he was also a New Yorker. So the two -- really the strong influences in Duke's band are native New Yorkers. Yes, they were.
Is that right? Was Duke, when he first came out, after Sonny Greer made the switch for him, and came out as Duke Ellington's Band, was the name of it -- overnight it was Duke Ellington's Band, right?

Yeah, yeah. How he got in the Cotton Club, see, I had been on tour with Wooding -- which we will talk about later on, and came back and we had been offered the job at the Cotton Club, and they offered us $1,100.00 a week which was a big salary then. And we said, 'No, we started in

Harlem, we're not coming back to Harlem. We've been to Russia we've played all over the world, we played for the kings and queens of the world, we're going to come back to Harlem?" Duke had his band together and organized and he took the job. He had a 10-piece band then, and he took the job. And the rest is history. That's how he got in the Cotton Club. I refused. I told Sam (unintelligible) "What should I do?" He said, "No, no, don't go back to Harlem." It was my decision not to go back to Harlem. After what we'd done we wanted to stay on top. We had no idea the potential of radio, we didn't know about radio. I don't think Duke did either, but he didn't have a job, he didn't have any preference. He hadn't been any place. But we, who had been all over South America and Europe and Africa, and the first jazz band ever to go to Russia and we had the distinction of being one of the most famous bands in Europe at that time -- the world for that matter, and we weren't coming back to Harlem -- we weren't about to come back to Harlem. We were going back in Vaudeville. We were preparing our stage band.
Right.
And had we known what radio could do,--
You would have taken advantage of it.
-- we would have given them $1,100.00 a week instead of them giving us $1,100.00.
Well, what we're doing now in this conversation is just leading up year through year, but I'll be

going back and pointing out some of the highlights about the trip to Russia, Africa and those kind of things. Just following the years now and touching upon some of these subjects. Now, during that -- after you disbanded your group -- you know, when you were with Liza --
And her Shuffling Sextet.
-- yeah, from there -- that particular band, five-piece band -- when it broke up did you settle in New York again?

Well, then I -- oh, yes, always back to New York, that's headquarters. In late '23 -- after Liza and her Shuffling Sextet -- let's see, I went -- I probably went back to Leroy's to work again. And Sam Wooding sent for me -- he was organizing a band to open up a new club in Harlem, which became world famous called The Nest --
Nest?
Nest, 1923.
Where was it located?

Oh, 133rd right off of Seventh Avenue. Incidentally, we used to entertain Roger Wolfe Kahn, Paul Whiteman, Henry Bussv, and all the royalty of Europe used to come there because they also had a review. It was a small nightclub called The Nest, and again, we had what they called then symphonic jazz band. We played the Nest, I guess a year or year and a half or so and the people heard us at Club Alabam.
Fletcher was leaving the Club Alabam.
What was your instrument --

Oh, let me tell you -- you see something we've omitted in '22, latter part -- or the middle of '22 -- organizing Fletcher Henderson's group for Ethel Waters. That was the next blues singer after Mamie.
Right, I want to touch up on a lot of things as we go along.

Yeah. Fletcher was a very important thing in what happened, because his first band was an eight-piece band -- we traveled on the road with Ethel Waters, did one nighters and also week stands at the TOBA Time, you know, black circuit. And in that band we had practically the same bunch out of Leroy's cabaret, plus more, and we had a baritone player from Memphis and Bill ? I remember. And we did that tour with Ethel Waters. And Fletcher then -- after we did that tour Fletcher came back and worked at a place called Cabaret at 129th Street and Lenox Avenue, that's where he hired Coleman Hawkins and organized his first band.
Is that right?

Yeah. Then he took the band from there to the club Alabam, in the meantime we were at The Nest, you see, with Sam Wooding's band. So, when Fletcher moved on to supposedly bigger things -- went from the Roseland to the -- I mean from the Club Alabam to the Roseland Ballroom on Broadway,
then we were the next band to go to the Club Alabam.
Was there quite a few bands at that time?
Oh, big bands, yes. All bands were big. Ten and more. That was during the big band era, all the 20's From the first -- after '22 the big bands started. Whiteman started the big band idea.
They were all pretty active, I mean there was --

Oh, yes, they all worked. They all worked. They made records or they worked on spots or big ballrooms. New York had -- well, the Roseland hired two big bands and the Rosemont in Brooklyn, the one at 53rd and Broadway hired two big bands. They were touring the country giving dances. The band business was just a billion dollar concern.
All that was before television and radio.
Before television and radio -- radio was coming on then, but television was unthought of. Nobody had dreamed of television.
Tell me about the TOB is it?
TOBA.
TOBA? What do those initials stand for?
Well, we used to say it was Take Old Man

Bailey's Advice. There was a guy who owned this time called Bailey, but I think it was -- I don't know what the legitimate names -- but TOBA -- that was the black vaudeville circuit, and many, many vaudeville teams originated -- some of them became headliners in the white circuit, some of them never went any farther than TOBA. [Theater Owners Booking Association]
There wasn't any of the white bands playing --
Oh, no, no, no, no. That was strictly a black action, you know, activity. Maurene, and Butter Beans and Suzy -- Ethel Waters played -- we played with Ethel Waters at TOBA.
Well, they had just a regular circuit.

Yeah, a regular circuit. From New York to Philadelphia, from Philadelphia all around the country, you know, as far west as Indianapolis, even Texas, Louisiana, Georgia, Florida, South Carolina, North Carolina, Virginia -- that's a circuit.
What instrument were you -- was your major instrument at that time?

Clarinet. Clarinet until I went into Sam Wooding's band and then I bought a saxophone in '23 -- I bought a saxophone. That was the first time I had a saxophone, but I'd been playing, you know, but the clarinet was my major instrument. Yeah. And after I went into Wooding's band I began
to -- I got a bassoon and I got an oboe and began to study oboe and bassoon. But prior to that clarinet was my instrument -- that's all I was playing.
What year was it that you went into the symphony band?
My first symphonic experience had to be in New York with a group called the Heights Symphony.
What year was that?
I was a bassoonist. That was in New York, that could have been 194 --
Oh, that was much later.
Oh, yes, much later, in the '40's. And from then on, you know, I went on from there to various things which we'll get to.
You played clarinet --
I played bassoon in the symphony, never clarinet, no.
I mean, you played clarinet until about '23 and you got your saxophone.
Saxophone then, then I took on the doubling and started doubling in '23.
In those years, yeah.
I can show you some pictures I had taken in '23 and '26 and all the different instruments and had the same things that I'm playing now.
And all those years up til -- you were mostly traveling with different groups?

Oh, yes, differant groups traveling. That was the thing to do, you had to travel. That's how you made your money. That was a pleasure then, with different bands on the road, one night stands, week stands, vaudeville week stands. That was the fun, meeting new women and meeting new musicians, and --
Enjoying the life of a musician.

Yes. I remember once in Louisville, Kentucky, we played a theater there -- this was with Ethel Waters, and after the first performance that night we went up this heavy-set, brown-skinned woman to cabaret next to the theater and said, "I sure likes the way you plays that long black stick." She said, "You like to come join our party?" Well, certainly, you know, sure I'll do anything. Well, it turned out this woman, she had about seven houses in Louisville. She was the biggest landlady in Louisville. Well, the last night we were in Louisville, she Shanghaied me.
Closing night.

Closing night she Shanghaied me at the -- met me at the stage door and put her razor up there and said, "You going to my house tonight, Bouchand ?" I said, "NO, we're going on to Chicago." "You ain't going to Chicago, you're going to my house."
Bouchand.

Bouchand. Put her razor here, and she was bigger than I am. I only weigh 145 soaking wet and she must have weighed about 180. And she said, "Bouchand, you going with me tonight." I said, "I got to go to Chicago." "You ain't going to go nowhere." And she put me in her Cadillac and then took me to the house. Well, I had my hand bag packed and my horns and so we're sitting up drinking and about 6:00 o'clock in the morning everybody's hungry. Of course, I'd been to her house several times during the week, but this was the last night. So, she said, "Bouchand, you hungry?" I said, "Yes." This was 6:00 o'clock, it was daybreak then. She went out in the kitchen to fix some ham and eggs because all the girls had gone to bed and all activity had stopped you know. Incidentally, her husband was an Army lieutenant and he came in while we were there about 3:00 o'clock that morning, and she let him in the front and said, "Don't worry about him." In those days I used to carry a gun from the circus, so this guy was a Captain, not a lieutenant, a Captain in the Army and she whipped him. She broke up, you could hear the chairs breaking and the wash bowls being, you know, you had a porcelain wash bowl and pitcher in your room then. Didn't have no running water in the room. She broke wash bowls, you could hear him hollering and screaming and heard the front door open. I thought it was she going out, it was he going out.
(unintelligible)

She cleaned him, she cleaned him. So it's 6:00 o'clock in the morning and she said, "Bouchand, you our trumpet player hungry?" And Gus Akin was with me and we said, "Yeah." So she went out in the kitchen to fix some bacon and eggs and I said, "Gus, I'm going." He said, "Oh, you can't do that," and I said, "I'm going." While she's fixing the eggs I got my horn under one arm, my hand bag under the other, and put my pistol inside of my case and I ran 15 blocks to the railroad station. Flew through the door and went right to the men's toilet and just fell out cold. So I told one of the porters there, if you see so and so, I called her name -- if you see her, you didn't see me. I hid in the -- and sure enough she came to the railroad station. I hid until the Chicago train came in. When the Chicago train came I skidded out and got on that train and went to Chicago. But here's what she had been doing. You know, Louisville's a great betting town. She put a fresh $300.00 and $400.00 in my pocket every day. "How much you got?" "I've got about $500.00 here." "Give me that, take another $300.00, some fresh money, that's old money take some new (unintelligible) money She's giving me in money." So I had about $1,500.00 (unintelligible) Sure enough showed up and went to Chicago.
That's a lot of money.
And I ran 15 blocks, too.
But you did escape.

I did escape, yeah, soon as I could get away, because she'd have killed me, no kidding. I didn't go back to Louisville until she died, you know. I made sure I was with Calloway, and we were going to Louisville, and I said, "Does such an such a person --?" "Oh, no, she's dead." "Oh, well, I'll go then."
You were safe.
That was in '36. That almost 12 or 14 years later.
You mentioned a couple of times about even musicians carrying guns, and there was no real call for it was there?

Well, I would say it was more a show of fear. I used to go up -- when we were traveling on trains I used to wear a wing collar with the forehand tie, and a cap, and a shoulder holster and I walked up and down through the trains with my coat off and nobody ever challenged me one way or the other. I had a big automatic. I don't know if they thought I was a cop or what. I was awful young to be a cop but nobody ever challenged me.
Weren't you ever stopped for --
Oh, I was stopped once finally. I was stopped. Oh, yeah. I was stopped in -- and arrested.
To legally --
In Chicago.
Did you go register -- have the gun registered?
No, no. You didn't register guns in those days.
I see.

I think you got a permit, I think you got a permit in those days, but everybody carried them in show business -- everybody had a pistol. And, one morning we were leaving the restaurant and -- 31st and State, and three white men came across the street -- we were crossing the street going to the hotel on the corner and these three white men said, "Okay, buddy, stop it right there." So I hit (unintelligible) He said, "Hold it," and they all came out with guns, turned out they were cops. And they caught me with my pistol, that was it, they put the cuffs on me and put me in jail for three days before they'd even booked me.
Let me kind of curve this conversation since we're speaking this way, like you say, you did quite a bit of traveling throughout the country. It was the South as well?

Well, that's how come we left Fletcher. We left Fletcher with Ethel Waters in Chicago. That's because -- we was with Fletcher, you know, and I went to Chicago, we were going to play the Grand Theater with Fletcher and Ethel.
Was this about '23, '24?
This was the early part of '23 or latter

part of '22. I remember -- I'm a little twisted on this. It was before the fall because I went into New York at the Nest in '23, in the fall of '23.. It must have been the first part of the winter of '23 or the latter part of '22. And we left the band after I got out of trouble and paid the fine and got out of trouble for carrying the gun. They were going south, and three of us would not go south -- four of us wouldn't go south, so they had to hire musicians from Chicago to make that tour. And --
So that's as far south as you would go?

Oh, I wouldn't dare go south in those days. I had been south with the circus and that was enough for me. And, what happened was, we - it took all the money that I had and that the four of us had to get the two of us out of jail because we had to pay the policy - Pete and he had to pay the judge, and all that sort of thing. Get us off to keep from doing six months. So we had enough money to get from Chicago to Pittsburgh, the four of us. We didn't have another penny after that. So we went to the hotel where we had stayed previously doing one-night stands in Pittsburgh, and told the man what had happened. "We don't have any money." So, he says, well, stay here and see what I can do. Maybe I -- you want to get to New York." I said, "We've got to get to New York." We didn't have a penny. "Have you got anything to eat?" "No,"

we didn't have anything to eat, so he fed us. He said, "Look, there's a dance down at Duquesne Garden tonight. Why don't you go down there and play. Maybe you can pass the hat or something." So, the trombone player said, "Let's do that." So that night we went down to Duquesne Garden. We told the leader -- and Old Man Bailey went with us and said what had happened. We got up on the stand and played the Tiger Rag with their rhythm section -- we played the solos and passed the hat. Monk, you're sitting there but you're not going to believe this. We got to the penny, to the penny, our fare back to New York, for the four of us. Not one penny over. We had to borrow money from Old Man Bailey to pay our taxi cab fare to go the railroad station. Not one penny over.
Right to the penny.

Right to the penny. So we got on the train the next morning to go to New York and so we're practicing -- about noon we got out the horns, one was a violin, trumpet, trombone and clarinet. And we're fooling around and one of the porters came through and heard us. He went back and got the steward. The steward said, "Would you boys like to play on the train for dinner?"
Perfect timing.
You know, it took about 12 hours to go from New York to Pittsburgh on a train. We said, "Yeah, okay, we got nothing to do." He said, "Well, look, I can't pay you

but anything you want to eat you can have." "Okay," you know, we tried to play it cool, but we were so happy we were going to eat. So we went and played for dinner and we got through and had steaks and chicken a la king and anything we wanted to eat. So, when it came time for supper, he said "Same deal goes, fellows." And we played for supper that night, and we ate again.
They didn't allow you to pass the hat?

On the train, no, just food. Let me tell you, so we got to New York and we didn't have enough money to even telephone to tell my father to come down -- we had an old broken down Cadillac then -- telephone daddy to come down to pick up at the station. I had to borrow a nickle from the porter so I could call my father to come and get me at the Pennsylvania Station.
That's great. Now, in those early years that you were playing music, did you do -- was it strictly music? You didn't have to go out and get a day job to support --

Oh, no, no, no. Once you're a musician or an actor, then you became a professional. It wasn't -- you didn't have to subsidize it with anything. You know, you gave all of your effort to your profession in those days.
But there wasn't enough work to go around?

There was enough, yes. There was enough. There were many, many theaters and even in Harlem there were three theaters operating that had vaudeville and shows. The Lafayette had tab shows, reviews, and the Lincoln Theater had vaudeville. And even up at 145th Street, the Roosevelt, they were doing -- on Lenox Avenue -- not the Roosevelt, Crescent I believe, where Jack Johnson appeared later on. They did vaudeville. There were plenty of places to work. And then you had the Savoy, you had -- in Harlem you had the cabarets, you had the Happy Rooms, you had Connie's Inn, you had the cabarets on 125th Street. Harlem was an active place.
But were they any white musicians at all ever worked up in the --
White musicians -- they might hire name white bands to play the Apollo Theater. They may -- on midnight shows they may have a white musician come back.
The same Apollo Theater that's operating now?

Well, it used to be in the early days it was called the Hurting and Seaman's Burlesque Theater, Hurting and Seaman's Apollo. It was a burlesque house and they turned it into a black theater doing reviews, in 1933 -- that's when it opened, black shows.
I see. Well, did any of the black
musicians work downtown in New York?

Well, yes, sure we did. We worked the Roseland, I told you, we worked the Club Alabam, we worked what was formerly the Little Club. Negro musicians worked all over New York, all over New York, in the restaurants and the small clubs. They didn't work the Palais Royal -- that was the big one where the whites worked. That was a choice spot, but we worked the Arcadia, the Rose-Land, the Empire, I worked all those ballrooms. The Turf Club. Surely, black musicians worked all of them. Snowden's first band was Kentucky Club at 49th Street. Oh, yes, black musicians worked all over New York and they did the gig work for all the rich people -- the parties you know. The guys like Ford Dabney and Jim Europe, they had all the gig work. I was Lucky Roberts -- in the '30's I played with Lucky Roberts. We'd play for the Stokesbury's and the Goulds and the Vanderbilts and all them. We'd ride on their private cars and go from one town to the other just playing music on their cars. Go with them to Florida and go back.
When you say on their cars --
They had private cars. All rich people in those days had a private car. They had their own Pullman and their own dining car.
Train.
Yeah, train. Hooked their car right on to a train.
Oh, I see.
Yeah, they had their own private car. It was also a sleeper -- equipped for sleeping, dining, cooking all that. The Wainmakers, yes.
You say they just hooked their car right to the train --
Just hooked their car right to the train and go where they wanted to go.
I see.
That's the way the rich were in those days.
That was in the '30's.
In the '30's, yeah.
Well, how was it for -- well, like -- we're still talking about -- well, back in the depression -- that was like 'late '20's --
Yeah, well, if you wish to speak of that -- if you want to get through more incidents in '25, between '25 and '30, including Europe.
That's fine.
The European thing was in that era.
The first you had gone abroad when you went to Europe, right?
We left the Club Alabam in '25.
Who was that with?
It was Sam Wooding.
Sam Wooding's band.

And there was an agent, Arthur Lyons, who was a Russian, and he got in touch with other Russians who came to New York and put up the money to create a large Negro review to tour Europe. And we were organized -- incidentally, Duke Ellington wrote the music for this review, this show. And we had a show of 53 people. We first landed in Germany and we played Germany. Toured all of Europe, then we went to Russia. Stayed in Russia about -- almost a year.
Now, this was obviously by boat that you traveled.
By boat, yes, yes. No one had crossed the Atlantic by plane then.
Well, did you play on the boat?
We just rehearsed. No, we didn't play for any audience or anything. We just rehearsed on the boat.
I see.

One day we were rehearsing and a wave hit the boat and all the port holes were open and these girls had bought all these dresses on time -- I remember that, and when they got to Europe the salt water had hit these dresses and they couldn't wear any of them, and they sent word over to Europe to collect the money and these girls had to pay. One of the girls happens to be a very rich woman today. She lives in
Mexico. She married a fellow who was very rich and lives in Mexico today.
These girls were part of the --
Yeah, the chorus girls, yeah.
Your first stops were in Germany?
Germany, Berlin.
How were you received?

Received wonderfully well. The people thought it was great. Some of the Germans still had their effects of World War I in their minds and they objected to us being there because they said they had so much trouble with the Senegalese during the war and they didn't want to see any more black people. They were very -- but the people by and large received us beautifully.
What type of places were they -- theaters?

Oh, yes, theaters, theaters. The Admiral's Palace was our first stop. Then we went to Hamburg to a big theater there, and from there we went to, I remember, Stockholm, Sweden, and we played the circus and there's where I met the Crown Prince. I had a letter from the crown prince of Sweden who's now the present King, and he was the head of the Red Cross then. We played concerts and special command performances for them there. Then we went to Denmark and Denmark was a fabulous town. It was more active than Paris in

those days. Then back to Germany and so into Budapest and Hungaria, Austria, Switzerland -- we went all over Switzerland. Italy, France, Spain -- we did all the big towns in Spain. And then we went to Russia.
You were booked by a promoter from Germany --

No, he was a Russian, his name was Nianof, he was a Russian. And we stayed with the show until after Russia and then we left the show in Paris, and then we were on our own and we started free lancing in Paris.
I see. Well, in Russia, did it go over well?

Tremendously well. The people loved us, they would come to the theater after every performance and pick out different ones and say, 'I'd like for you to meet my family, would you come to my house for dinner?' Or, 'You and this fellow, come to me, I have daughters, would you like to meet my daughters, come to my house for dinner.' And on Monday night they would invite us to the Artist's Club and I had the pleasure of hearing a 105-piece symphony without a conductor. That was the first experiment. We heard that in '26.
105 pieces without a conductor?
105 pieces without a conductor. It was a tremendous experiment and it worked. But they were all concert maestros, all the guys that performed.
This was in Russia.
Moscow, yes. We'd go to the ballet. The Russian people were beautiful. They were absolutely beautiful to us.
They had no problem relating to the music?
Oh, no, no.
I mean, what I'm saying, they weren't familiar with the records, or were they at that time?

Records weren't an item in those days. It was in-person things, you see.. Records were just something incidental that people had. They had records, but they didn't relate from records as to your popularity. They'd go to see you in person. And we had recorded while we were in Berlin, we had made four numbers and I guess -- the distribution wasn't as great as it is now, they were just local things, maybe one country over and one country around, something like that. But they didn't know us from Adam, all they knew was this Negro Revue. And they had heard through reading and all about how Negro people danced and sang and how they played jazz.
How large a show was this, along with the band?
It was 53 people in the show.
Fifty-three people in all. And Duke Ellington wrote all the music?
