He wrote all the music. A fellow by the name of Joe Trent did the lyrics, libretto, and Arthur Lyons did the choral, Charlie Davis did the choreography, and it was staged by this Russian who is now in Hollywood, he's a big agent in Hollywood now, Arthur Lyons. Yeah. He staged the show.
Did you get an opportunity to hear some of the musicians in Europe and Russia?
Oh, I certainly did.
Some of the bands and groups --
Oh, my goodness, yes. Jazz, you see -- they tried to play jazz and they knew nothing of it. And what I heard was their music and I was impressed -- particularly the gypsies.
Were they playing some of the American songs?

Oh, yes, in Germany. In Germany, yes and Sweden, but they hadn't reached yet -- you see, we were sort of pioneers in jazz in Europe. Will Marion Cook and Bechet and a few others had been over there, but they hadn't traveled extensively -- they didn't travel extensively like we did, but they'd been to Russia but they didn't impress people. But we went there with a big show, a big band of 14 pieces and stage scenery, you know.
Very exciting.

Yeah, very exciting. And we were playing different -- in our reed section we had about 25 horns and our trumpet players were playing French horns and the trombone. We had a tremendous big band, big stage band. We had a real stage band and we sang.
What were prices like to come to see the band in Europe? Did they pay much more than they would pay here?

Yes. Those days people were paying an unheard of price of $5.00 admission, you know, and that's 40, 50 years ago, $5.00 admission, but this was an unusual thing. Don't forget, it was from America and they'd pay $5.00 to hear it. Ordinarily, they'd just pay $1.00 to hear their own attractions. That was the difference. Yes, they paid good money.
(What were the (unintelligible))
turnouts, then.
Oh, yes. Packed houses, packed houses.
At those prices.

Yes, we packed them. It's the biggest thing that ever hit Europe in that part of the '20's. That was before any of the big bands ever went there. We were the first large band to play in Europe. The first, the first.
Again, what year was that?
'25 we went to Europe, and '26 when we got to Russia.
How long did that tour last?
Well, we came back in '27. I went back again the latter part of '27 and I stayed until, let me see, '28, then I came back, and Sam went back and he stayed.
You actually --
Yes, Sam went back and stayed again, and I left in '28.
It lasted for a year?
Oh, no, two years and something. Two years -- from '25 til '27. In the meantime we'd been to South America, too, you know. Buenos Aires.
But I mean during that two years, you were in Europe traveling?
Yes, yes.
Two years?
Yes.
So, you were -- undoubtedly you made some return engagements.
Oh, yes, yes, we did.
Did you travel mostly by train after you were there?
Always train, no cars, no busses. always trains.
Yeah, with that large a group I guess you had to -- had your own cars and --
Yes, and , you know, they have classes in
Europe, your first class, second class and third class. Third class is a hard bench, you know.
Yeah.

We -- they did us a dirty trick. Going from Lithuania to Moscow they bought us third class passages. We had so many people, you know, and they were trying to cut corners. And I rode those hard benches from Lithuania -- it took us two and a half days to get to Moscow and I rode a hard bench for two and a half days and I got to Moscow and I couldn't sit down and I couldn't stand up.
Well, what happened in those two years if you needed a replacement?

There was nosuch thing as a replacement. Tommy Ladner left us and that's it, he left, period. Instead of having three trumpets we had two. There was no such thing as a replacement. We got back to Paris -- you could always get a replacement in Paris because there were a lot of black musicians in Paris. That was the headquarters, but in Russia, Germany and those places, there was no replacement.
Who had -- which country, if you can recall, had closer to the best concept of them playing jazz?
I would say, then, the Frenchmen. The Frenchmen --
They came close.
Yes, because they had been exposed to it

longer than anyone else, because the black musicians went to France. They didn't go to Germany. They didn't go to Russia. They didn't go to -- later they spread into Sweden and Germany, but France was the headquarters. All the black musicians of Europe went to Paris. The Frenchmen were really exposed to it first, and it spread from there, yeah.
We have quite a few musicians today from the States that are actually living in parts of Europe, that have made it their home. Was it pretty much the same back then?

Yes, there were. When we got there there were black musicians living and had been there for years. Spoke French like natives. We found some in England, a few in England. England in those days was rather prejudiced, and it wasn't too good for -- they were racial conscious and it wasn't too good for black musicians. They'd listen to you. Our biggest flop was when we opened in London at Holburn's Empire. We flopped all over the place and we couldn't understand it. We'd been a sensation all over Europe, even in Manchester in Northern England we'd played and we went over very big. We opened in London at Holburn's Empire and we were an absolute flop. We bombed all over the place. We thought it was because we were following another black act and wemade them split the thing up, you know. But we didn't do good in London at all. Didn't do good at all, we were a little bit too classy. We were dressed in striped

trousers, you know, and oxford grey coats and ties, and if we'd been slapstick I think it would have been great. But we had a very classy organization and Europe had rubbed off on us, you know, and they wanted to see a black orchestra doing comedy and slapstick things, you know, and we didn't do that. So, we didn't do good in England at all. Never went back either. Never returned to England. Haven't been to England since.
But the rest of Europe was pretty --
Oh, sensational, South America was sensational.
Did you go to Africa, any parts of it?
Yes, we played the Shepherd's Hotel in Cairo, Egypt, in '27. We had a two-week engagement, two weeks.
In Egypt.
Yes.
Well, what parts of northern Africa were you touching? Any parts of Tunisia, Algiers, Casablanca?
Well, not in those days, but I'd say recently, because in 1964 I was at those places.
I see, but back then --
Back then, no. We just went directly to Cairo.
Well, when you left Europe to come back to the States, obviously the band broke up, or did it?
Well, no, it didn't exactly. We went

from Europe to -- we went from Marseilles to Buenos Aires and we stayed in South America for about six months. There we played Buenos Aires, Montevideo, Rosario, Tucumán, and one other town -- we played vaudeville and we also played cabaret. We played theaters there and cabarets. We played at the Cabaris in Buenos Aires.
How was your reception there?
Great, great, wonderful.
Well, was it -- did you get -- did you gain momentum from that band by going to Europe and Russia and back -- when you come back to the States after leaving the country was it like --

Well, naturally, we were youngsters and we were highly impressed with the people and the attitude and the mannerisms of Europeans and we sort of took on some of that and we assumed some of that air. And we didn't fall back into the same groove that we had been in when we left, because we were more matured, but some of Europe had rubbed off on us and we felt that we were something special.
So, when you got back home --

And I did some studying. I studied bassoon in Germany, I studied clarinet in France, and we felt as though we had arrived, you know. That's why we wouldn't take the Cotton Club for $1,100.00 a week back in Harlem. Get out, don't insult us. There was many a day came about later on we
But, I mean, didn't it make you a more prestigious group here in the States when you came home? After traveling abroad?
Oh, yes, yes. We went vaudeville immediately. We formed a new act and got some new personnel. We formed a very class act and we did vaudeville, just the band with no --
With the chorus girls and the whole business?
No, no, just band.
Just band?

Concert, band, just our band. Band alone. Sam Wooding and his orchestra. And we toured -- we did theaters, just band. And didn't, you know, introduce -- in the early days of vaudeville when we did vaudeville acts, we did a vaudeville act with the band before we went in the Cotton Club. They put cards up for the next number. You didn't open your mouth, you didn't say a word. Play a tune, the card went out for the next number, and people come just to hear your music. Didn't have to sing or dance. But when we formed our new group after Europe, we sang, we had quartets, we had solos, we had comedy, we had effect. We had a railroad thing we did where the whole stage moved and the band was imitating a train, close your eyes and you'd swear you hear a train.
Was this music written by Duke that you were playing?
Oh, no, no, this wasn't Duke when we came back. After we left the show, this was Sam Wooding. Sam was quite a composer and arranger.
Oh, I see.
Oh, yeah, he still is. Incidentally, he's still going. He's 82 years old and he's still going.
Is that right. That's great.

Yes, he's still going in New York. He has organized a band and he said, 'Well, Duke's gone and all of them are gone and I'm going to take up where they left off.' He's 82 years old and still going. He has a band, too, in New York. He's working. Big band. He does engagements whenever he can get them.
Well, after Sam's band, did you go for yourself again?
I left Sam's band when the vaudeville got slow and I joined a show called Keep Shuffling with Miller and Lyle and Sissle and Blake.
The show called Keep Shuffling. It didn't use anyone's name in particular.
No, they they were the stars of the show because I had -- I did a stint with them when they had Shuffle Along in New York -- that was in 1920. Incidentally, we went

over that, we passed by that. But I played part -- I played a few weeks in that show, but I didn't want to be tied down to a show because I couldn't have no fun sitting in a pit. If I could be on stage I could have a ball on stage. And this Keep Shuffling -- I joined them and went on the road with that show. We did 17, 18 weeks in New York, then we went on the road with it. And the show was owned by Arnold Rothstein, he was the great gambler, you know. So, while we were in Chicago he was murdered at Park Central Hotel and naturally the show closed because there was nobody -- no owner of the show. He was a gangster, you know, Arnold Rothstein. And so, that closed the show. We had a very successful show, too. I decided to stay in Chicago a while. I worked with the Dreamland, Sunset, some of the Chicago bands, and I got lonesome for New York and just all of a sudden I told the leader that my mother was very sick and I had to go back to New York. In those days you loved New York. You didn't like to stay away from New York too long. New York was just like being in heaven. Everything in the world was there, all the activity was there, anything that happened in the world, it happened in New York. If you could do something in New York, -- and do something, New York was the place to sell it. Not as it is today -- people are running from New York. People in the world were running to New York in those days.
In those days, it's like during the period you were in Chicago, Chicago was fairly active, though.
Yes, but it was a haven for gangsters. That was the period the gangsters took over Chicago -- those days.
I see.

You could sit in your house any night in Chicago and hear a huge explosion down the block -- some tailor shop that didn't pay off for protection or a grocery store -- they bombed them. As a matter of fact, I worked for Ralph Capone at a place -- at the Sunset -- it was owned by Ralph Capone.
Did you ever see him or meet him?
Yes, I saw Ralph. I didn't see his brother, the other Capone, but Ralph Capone I saw many times.
Then you got so lonely for New York you had to go back?
Oh, yes, I couldn't stay in Chicago. Couldn't take it. I couldn't take it.
What other cities, with the exception of New York, did you spend any time at in terms of to live there, to settle there?
No, never, never. Until I left in '66 to go to Puerto Rico. New York was always headquarters. WE pulled up stakes in '66 and went to Puerto Rico to live.
You never found another town that you could actually live and be comfortable in?

No, no, Puerto Rico we found very good. We enjoyed it, and my young children were born there and I had a good opportunity there -- I worked in the symphony there. And at that time I'd had -- I'd done a few concerts. I did one as an addition in the Philharmonic. I also worked with the Orchestra Metropolitan as an addition under Demetri Metropolis. I played contrabassoon. But because I was a bassoonist, they used me as a showcase. And they put me -- I also went in Radio City later on as a showcase. They said, 'Oh, yes, we hire black musicians, look at Garvin Bushell.' You see? Musicians --
Right.
I went to station WJZ and I signed up and I signed up my instruments and naturally I wasn't playing flute, and so I got a call from Paul Whiteman to come join his orchestra.
Are we back now in the early '30's?
No, we're ahead of that, we're a little ahead of that, but you led me into that by what happened in New York.
Yeah, I was going to take you back now because I want to get -- I want to go step by step.

But Whiteman, after he found out who I was, he refused to hire me. But the name Bushell tricked him, you see, and he found a bassoon and oboe and those things, so in order to get me out of it he said, 'But you don't play flute,

do you?" I said, "Well, you know I don't play flute." "Yeah, but the contract," he couldn't speak English hardly, "in the Contract it calls for a flute." You know. I had a friend of mine who was a bassoonist and didn't play flute either and he got the job with Whiteman and paid $300.00 a week. And had 15 weeks booked, but Whiteman wouldn't hire me because he found out I was black.
What year was this?
That must have been '47, '48, as late as '48.
I see.
Yeah, station WJZ.
Well, let's go back, if I may, because I'm anxious to find out about the years that you got involved for the first time in symphony -- am I right in saying the years of the early '30's?
Yes, well --
When you first experienced --

No, my first experience with truly symphonic work began in the '40's with the Height Symphony and I had a good bit of training from a former member of the Philadelphia Orchestra. He used to be an oboe player with the Philadelphia Orchestra, Maxim Waldo, and he was the conductor of the Height Symphony, and I went there twice a week.
Well, I didn't mean to jump from the
period of the late '20's over to the '40's. I'd like to hear about the '30's --
Well, the '30's --
--because -- am I right in saying that it was the period of your first acquaintance with --
Yes, so much went on in the '30's.
Yeah, right in the '30's. Cab Calloway and --
Oh, yes, my. In the '30's, the very first part of '30's was a little rough because business was dying down and the big bands were struggling to hang on.
Was that caused by -- during the depression?

The depression was in '29, see. I mean the crash was in '29, and the effects of it was in '31,'32 -- that was real depression -- '33 -- and then we were working gigs in New York for $7.00 a night. Seven Dollars for a gig, and glad to get it. Ten Dollars you had a tremendous gig. Then we went on -- I finally got a job. They hired me at the Arcadia Ballroom with a band the name of Charlie Turner. That was the million dollar ballroom. I stayed there quite some time.
How large was that band?
I must have been with that band until I rejoined Fletcher.
Was it a large band?

Yeah, big band. I rejoined Fletcher -- yes, I was with that band and even the band after we left Arcadia, we were the second band to go into the Apollo Theater and I was the house arranger. I did the arranging for the production numbers. And we stayed there quite some time.
And when you say you were the house arranger there for the --
Apollo Theater.
-- Apollo Theater, that was just strictly for -- they were having bands, or did they have shows at that time?
They had shows, yes, they had shows.
It was pretty much like the --
Yes, just like -- yes, shows, productions.
-- like Amateur Hour and that type of thing?

Amateur Hour, yes. Then they had productions, chorus lines, comedians, and they had production numbers, and I used to do the arranging for the production numbers. Like you have the big show numbers here with the girls on the pedestals, you know.
Sure, well this is where Ella got her first discovery.
No, hers was in the M&S Theater down the
street from the Apollo.
Oh, I see.
It was the M&S Theater. See, there were three vaudeville theaters right on 125th Street within one block -- the M&S, the Apollo and Loei's Victoria.
And there was enough business forall three?

Sure, sure. My goodness, people went to theaters. They didn't have television -- there was nothing else for them to do. See, you had to go somewhere with something visual in order to lighten up the burdens, you see? Depression was still on in the '30's.
Then you stayed on at the Apollo then, writing arrangements?
I stayed at the Apollo from '30 to '34, then I left the band and I joined a fellow by the name of Fess Williams, his band, and I traveled a while with him on the road.
Were these people that you -- different bands like Fess --
Fess Williams.
Fess?
Fess, yeah, he's from Louisville, Kentucky. He used to be the master of ceremonies at Chicago Theater. Not Chicago, but the South Parkway Theater, the big theater on the south side.
Were they of name -- recording -- did they have records out?
Yes, oh, Fess was -- yes, Fess made records and a great road band. Everybody in the country knew Fess. Great road band man.
Were there much of -- dances at the time? Did they play dances?

Dances -- that's what you played -- dances. Dances were packed. We used to play -- we played to audiences of 12,000 and 14,000 people. I remember in New Orleans one night the race track -- we had 11,000 people with Calloway. That's just to dance, 11,000. In Atlanta, Georgia, one night -- no, Baton Rouge, we had 4,000 people. This was Chuck Webb. Many times we had 3,000 and 4,000 people at a dance.
Now, you speak about the towns in the south, were they a mixed audience?
No, no, no.
How did they -- how was that --
If it was a black dance, there would be white spectators who were not allowed to dance. If it was a white dance, then they didn't have black spectators.
If it was a white dance, it was just white.
Yeah. Let me tell you something. This is very peculiar. I remember seeing -- speaking about that -- in

Greenville, South Carolina, or Charleston -- they had three ropes -- two ropes at the hall. They had a rope that -- the hall cut off in three sections. One section in the middle was for the white dancers. This section was for the blacks. This section over here was for the mulattos. You see, there's a great mulatto cast in Greenville, Mississippi, and Charleston, South Carolina. The Mulattos stayed over here because they thought they were better than the blacks, because all their daddies was ex-slave owners, you know. All their daddies had to be white, so naturally they thought they were better than the full-blooded blacks. And it was cut off in three sections, and nobody better not cross his rope. If you wanted to stay in that hall, you better not cross that rope.
The mulattos was on the right, the whites in the middle, and the blacks on the far --
That's right.
Well, I guess they had -- they were -- learn and adjust to live with that and were satisfied with it as a way of life.
They understood it. They'd been, you know, it was their way of life in the south. Referring to that --
But they all enjoyed the same music coming from the stage.
All coming from -- the same music, same

music. And speaking about that way of life, I went to play with the Post family in South Carolina. They were a very rich people who conditioned race horses, you send your horses down there to be conditioned. It's an old southern family. And there were two fellows who met us at the train -- this was with Lucky Roberts and there were about five -- four or five of us to play his New Year's gig down there. Just for one night. Two fellows -- one was a mulatto sort of Negro and the other was a white man. So, I happened to be in the car with the white man and the rest of the boys -- well, there was two or three in my car and there was two or three in the other car with this mulatto Negro. So, this white fellow says, "See that fellow driving that car over there?" He said, "That's my brother. That's Charlie Post. There ain't a better man that ever walked this green earth. That's my brother over there. His daddy was my daddy." Now, that situation is all over the South in those days. We saw it very prevalent in the south,and in Greenville, Mississippi, and Charleston, South Carolina you saw that. The Posts -- the mulatto Posts had charge of all the servants and horses and stables. He ran that. He had his separate house on the plantation. He didn't live in the big house, but he said, "There ain't a better man ever walked this green earth, and that's my brother." And he was a Negro.
Well, we were saying, that's their way of life (unintelligible)
The way of life -- that's why I brought that up, because -- and they understood it. They understood it.
Well, you know, I go back a ways in music and I can remember back when the musicians were highly regarded as a special kind of people. They were really --

Yes, they were. It was quite an honor to be a musician then, Monk. You felt as though you were somebody because people considered you as such and musicians were sort of conscious of that and they carried themselves accordingly. In later years they didn't. It began in the '30's when they began to lose their sense of value and culture -- I don't know, it began to be just like anybody else. I went with Fletcher in '35 and --
This is Fletcher Henderson?

Yeah, I went back with Fletcher in '35 and we went on -- in the latter part of '34 and in '35 we went to Chicago to play in a cabaret out there. I found out that musicians in Chicago -- there were quite a few of them stranded. They wanted to put them out of hotels because of their deportment and musicians would then -- the dignity -- they'd lost all of it. As the younger ones came in -- the older ones knew how to deport themselves, but the younger ones came in and the dignity wasn't part of their profession at all. So, I was with Fletcher in '35 and while I was with Fletcher, Cab sent me -- called me up and said would I like to join the band. That was in '35.

Fletcher owed me money, so I just quit without notice -- I gave him notice (unintelligible) Cab offered me $125.00 a week and with Fletcher most of the time on the road I got nothing. So, since Fletcher was a personal friend of mine, he'd been with me for many years -- as a matter of fact, he lived in my house when he came to New York.
Is that right?

Oh, yes. We met him at the train when he came from Atlanta after he graduated from Atlanta University. He came to our house to live. His aunt roomed at our house so he come right there to live with his aunt in hour house. So I'd known Fletcher since he first -- in the '20's when he first came to New York. So, when the money was short I was the first one that didn't get paid. "Oh, Garvin, you know you'll get yours later on." I was the straw boss and the straw boss always catches it. I was the straw boss. He'd walk off the stage, "Garvin, play the next two sets."
What was the problem financially? He made it didn't he?
Well, something happened. Sometimes we made it and sometimes we didn't, on the road.
But it wasn't because he, for example --
The band was always a sensation, but sometimes the dances weren't promoted well, you know, some dances flop, I don't care if you have stars, you know.
It wasn't the case that he'd lost his race track or anything like that?
No, he didn't gamble -- he couldn't gamble, he didn't hardly gamble.
Okay.
Fletcher was as timid as a mouse.

Well, I led into a question because I was going to ask something and hopefully lead into another one. The one question I was asking about the dignity of the musicians in those days. Like in the South, when you were in the South, because of the high quality dignity that a musician carried, it didn't help him in the south-- the black --

Well, on the contrary, Monk. Let me give you an example. I never had any trouble in the South and you know why -- I approached the southerner with an air that I felt that I was his equal, if not better. And when I began speak, I spoke in the best English that I knew how, with the presence of -- I had confidence in myself. I never backed up. I walked into stores in Texas where they didn't even allow black porters, and I said, 'How do you do?' You know, they said, 'Where you from?' 'I'm from New York, does it make any difference?' Loud, see. I used to disarm them that way.
With authority you would --
Yes, with authority. I went in and I never backed up in the South, but I didn't go where I thought
Sure.

I remember in Hinton, some boys stood up and the Greek made them take off their hat at the door, or they went hungry. I went hungry. I told them I'd eat anything in the road before I'd go in there and buy a sandwich. They stood there and took off their hats and waited until he cooked them a sandwich. Well, I went hungry. I was so hungry I couldn't hardly talk. I wouldn't go in there. But, when I had to go somewhere I found out you could disarm them down there by just doing another act. You know, put on a different act, and when they found out you weren't from there, it was a different story. Never had any trouble.
Well, that's exciting to hear.

That's the way I got along in the South. I was always afraid, though. I was very nervous. We had a big fight one night in Johnson, Tennessee, and I was frightened to death that they'd beat up every black person in there and said, 'You boys go out the back door because we're going to kill the rest of them here tonight.' And they shot them up and they beat them, they beat them to a pulp. I was always afraid. That's why it was a hard time getting me to go south. I know I can just take so much and that's it.
I would imagine that's pretty much of a general feeling at the time.
But it's so -- thank God it's changed.
Yes, it's behind us now. We're all happy about that.
I was recently in the South and it's behind us. It's beautiful in the South now. Beautiful -- the people are beautiful. I just came across from Florida -- all the way across, through Mississippi --
A lot of that is hard to believe and I'm sure everybody feels pretty much the same way and they're happy about that.
-- the people are just beautiful. It's beautiful.
Okay, I wanted to ask too -- you mentioned leaving Fletcher to go with the Cab -- Cab Calloway that is.
Yes, yes.
That must have been a beautiful experience.
It was. That was the highlight -- that band was the biggest thing in show business. When he sent for me I just left, because --
This must have been about the middle '30's, right?
'35 when he sent for me, winter of '35.
Now, he was familiar with you, your
playing --

Well, see, my friend was over there from -- Claude Jones -- we went to Wilberforce together, and he was familiar with my playing, so they hired me to play the first alto. And I stayed two years in the band.
You traveled with Cab Calloway for two years?
Oh, yes, two years. I did two seasons in the Cotton Club with him. You know, the new Cotton Club downtown.
He was a big draw, Cab was.

Oh, one of the biggest. I tell you, we had nine thousand people in New Orleans the first time he was there. We had 11,000 people at the race track underneath the grandstand -- the dancefloor had 11,000 people. Yes, yes. Cab was a big sensation all over the country. I can tell you an incident that happened. We were in a town called Longview, Texas. In those days we traveled, even Cabby traveled in two cars. We had a baggage car and a pullman, that's how we traveled. And we're on the side track lying up in upper berths in Longview, resting, so a fellow came aboard and said, 'I'm the fellow that's going to run the dance here tonight. It's a rough town, everybody's got money here, they just had a new oil strike, and they got money. It's going to be a little rough. But I'm going to look out for you guys. Don't worry, I'm

going to have the sheriff and six deputies there." I said, "By God, what you got here?" He said, "Well, it's tough. I came here from Georgia with my colored boys and I carried my little arrow head pistol and I protected them. Same as I'm going to protect you all tonight." So he said, "Don't worry. They're going break up -- they're going to fight. They're going to fight all over the place -- they got money." This was a white we were playing for, too. So, sure enough, we got way out to this road house, way out on the road, and we got our bus to take us there and we saw all these sheriffs in their hats and the deputies. "How you doing, Boys?" You know, down south you're a boy, even if you're 90 years old, you're a boy. Fine. So we got on the stage and played the first set. Normal, normal. So during intermission the guy said, "Now, you bays don't go outside. There's a cellar door right down here, you all go down the celler during intermission." And so he put us in the cellar. While we're down there, man, it sounds like a tornado's going -- rumble, chairs, hollering, screaming, bottles, and he poked his head down and said, "They're fighting like dogs, don't come up." Oh, they were cleaning out the place. So, finally, the sheriff got them settled down and by that time they're drunk. So we went back up on the stand after intermission. One guy came dancing along and he had seven $100.00 bills spread out like this -- incidentally, all the sheriff and all his deputies right in front of the bandstand -- they didn't move from there.
He said, "Sheriff, if you just move out the way and let me hit that so and so in the mouth one time, you can have all these -- you can have all this money."
You're kidding!
He offered the sheriff $700.00, said, "I want to hit him in the mouth just once," talking about Cab. Sheriff says, "What you want to hit him for?" "I just want to hit him because he's who he is."
They had that much envy?

Oh, yeah, yes, they were vicious. So, the sheriff took -- and all the sheriffs had marks and one of them had an eye closed and they had cops there too, you never saw such fighting people in your life.
But they did protect you?

Oh, they did. They better had, they'd have ruined us. So, pretty soon -- we're sitting down -- better take anotherintermission. Got a little rough, but take another one before you play the last tune. So, while we're sitting downstairs in the cellar, I heard this, "Take your hands off of me." And we had three valets, one of them used to stay at one end of the bandstand, and the others at the two ends. Well, they were kind of timid. So, one of them, the big valet we had was right at the door to keep anybody from coming down. So, I heard, "Take your hands off me." Our valet said, "You can't go down there." He says, "You're in Texas. You don't tell me

what I can't do. Take your hands off me." I said, "Oh, oh, Bushell this is your time." I'm right near the door. Something just -- just told me. I don't know what made me do it. Normally, I should have been hiding somewhere behind the door. I walked, went up the stairs and here this white fellow's trying to get down and Harold's got his hand on him. He said -- I said, "What's the problem?" "Well, this so and so wants to keep me from going down here to see Cab, you know, we loves Cab down here and I want to go talk with him. You going to keep me from going down there?"
(End of first side of tape.)
Mr. Bushell, what other town do you recall visiting that was exciting?

Well, being an auto bug brings to my mind our engagement in Southern Rhodesia, Salisbury, to be exact. You know, that's the country where they have the double standard, you know, one standard for Africans and one standard for the non-Africans. There are signs on all the buildings saying that we reserve the right to exclude whom we wish, meaning that they can throw you out on your ear when they're ready. And there were three blacks in the orchestra. But our State Department had briefed us previously, saying, 'if you have any trouble, that's just what we want, but I don't think they'll do anything.' Which they didn't. We went wherever the white musicians went and we stayed. There were no incidents at all.
But I remember one night Benny Morton -- Remember Benny Morton, the trumbonist?
Oh, yes, yes.

Well, we went down to the grill to have a sandwich and a glass of beer and there were four or five fellows sitting over in the corner. I had on my blazer with the emblem of the Sports Car Club of America, and they saw that and said, "Hey, you belong to the Sports Car Club of America?" I said, "I certainly do." I pulled out my credentials and showed them. "Come on, have a seat." Well, it turned out, in their minds, Sports Car Club of America -- they have great regard for the Sports Car Club of America. To them it's just the greatest automobile club in the world. And they found out that there was a black American that belongs to the sports car club and they had -- they accepted me with open arms. And sat down and said, "Tomorrow, we're having the -- one of our biggest meets. Would you like to attend? Would you like to come out?" I said, "Certainly would." "All right, see you tomorrow, come out to the gate and just ask for me, or if you forget the name, either one of us -- some of us will be there." Sure enough, Benny And I went out to the race track the next day and one of the -- two of the fellows were at the gate and they drove us back in one of the race cars to their starting tower, you know, and took us up there and introduced us to the judges and what not. Believe me, this is the first time a black man ever stepped foot in the
Premier?

No, I just called his name. Well, that thought escapes me. Anyhow, it was his palace -- it will come to me. And you know, Zanzibar is the largest exporter of spices in the world -- the peppers and ginger and cinnamon -- comes from Zanzibar, and the fellows who load those ships -- these bags, they have done it so long til their skin has turned the color of cinnamon -- into the skin and it doesn't wash out. They're a yellowish-brown -- a yellowish-brown, and the head and their shoulders and bodies and through the whole system -- they can't live long. But only certain people do that and they have turned the color of the cinnamon and the powder, they've done it for so long. Another interesting feature in Zanzibar was all the banks have large, mahogany doors with golden spikes on them. So, we inquired what were those spikes about. They said, 'Well, years ago when a guy wanted to break in -- sultan in the sultan's palace or one of his banks -- they just bring the elephant and push the door down and go on in and rob the bank.' So they put big golden spikes on every bank -- there's spikes that protrude at least a foot and a half of solid gold
on the fronts of all banks or any big business store, they put these big spikes to keep the elephants from pushing the doors in. The elephants won't go into those spikes. Fantastic.
Discourage the elephants.

And gold too, gold. Zanzibar is quite a place, it's a very romantic place. You know, all writers have written about Zanzibar, especially those sea tales. But we went all the way over there to play for a beauty contest that lasted about an hour and a half and got on our planes and went back to Dar es Salaam.
The beauty contest -- where were the beauties actually gathered from? All over --
Well, they're beautiful women because they're a mixture of East Indian and Oriental.
I see, not from Africa?

No, from that section, Zanzibar. From Zanzibar -- Zanzibar's quite a good size island. And we went from there to the Island of Madagascar which is the largest island in the world, I believe -- or almost the largest, next to Greenland, I believe. They call it Malagash. They speak French there. That's the only place in the East that -- we found -- the large place that they spoke French rather than English. And they have a combination of Oriental and Chinese -- I mean Indian and Chinese culture. They don't consider themselves African at all. They don't want any part of Africa, yet they
-- and they push rickshaws like Chinese and yet they look -- some of them look Chinese -- they're a mixture. I have some film. Sometime if you come over to my house I'll show some of these films.
I'd be happy to see them.

And Morton and I were going -- and the women are beautiful. You can stand on the corner and just see the most beautiful women you ever laid eyes on. So, we went back to Dar es Salaam and from Dar es Salaam we went back to Nairobi, and from Nairobi we caught a plane and crossed the Sahara again and went back to Morocco, Rabat and Casablanca, And we spent a few days buying souvenirs. I bought a couple of big tables. I think that table you see in my house -- that round table -- I bought that in Casablanca. No, in Rabat and then Medena. And then we got a plane back to Paris, and who was my guest coming back from Paris and sat in the seat with me, Robert Goulet. And we ya-ya'd all the way back on the plane.
That's great. He had engagements at that time --

Well, he was riding first class, but we held up the plane in Paris for an hour making this connection from Rabat to Paris -- they held up the plane coming to New York for an hour. So he came back and said, 'I want to see who held up my trip an hour.' And we've got on African safari hats and safari jackets and sunburn and husky -- you know, three months

in the bush and you show it. Some guys had fez on. He said, 'What is this back here?' 'Well, we are the Great American Band.' 'Musicians?' 'Yeah.' So he sat down in my seat and we ya-ya'd all the way back, with Taubman and Artie Baker and some more of them. We had an incident the first night in Senegal. We had a trumpet player with us. He was a Jewish boy but a great trumpet player. You've heard him on the Jackie Gleason program many, many times. Anyhow, he got out of the cab one night and -- in Senegal in Dakar, and refused to pay the bill. That's something you don't do in Africa. You don't do that -- well, I'm telling you, the whole police force came to the hotel that night -- 2:00 o'clock in the morning and woke everybody. They were going to put us out of Africa the first night. And had not it been for our advance man -- our manager, Taubman, the conductor, was going to send him back to the States. He had a lot of trouble. And all over Africa, he put on the fez and he looked like an Arab so -- light skinned Arab, but he was Jewish out of New York. I think he resides now in Florida, but he's a very prominent trumpet player, I won't call his name. And, but the Africans are very strict, you know. They put in jail in Africa and they just forget you're there. You know, that's the end of your life, you finish there.
But all in all it was a successful trip?
Oh, yes, yes. I'll tell you, I saw more
poverty in Africa than I've ever seen any place in the world. (unintelligible) The conditions in Africa among the poor and the people in the bush -- I don't see how they live.
They don't have an in between -- it's either rich or they're poor.
It's either the upper class or the bush -- people from the bush.
Yeah.

The country folks, they call it the bush. And you haven't seen poverty until you see it in Africa. Children with these bloated stomachs and all that -- it's pathetic. So if you hear anybody talk about refusing to give aid to Africa, they don't know what they're talking about, because they need it badly. And they're great people, you know. They're wonderful people. With all their poverty, they're as dignified as you've ever seen anything in your life. They don't bend, they don't stoop. Great people. When it comes to roots, I admire my roots. So, we finally got the plane and came back to the States.
Can I ask you -- the trumpet player you were speaking about that performed with Jackie Gleason, was that Bobby Hackett?
Oh, no, no. I played with Bobby in Puerto Rico. No, that wasn't Bobby.
The late Bobby Hackett, it wasn't him?
No, no, Bobby was a great guy. Bobby
wouldn't do a thing like that. This guy that did that, you know you've heard his name -- but I'm a little reluctant to mention his name on tape.
Okay. And after you finished your tour there in Africa --
Went back to Ryans, back to Jimmy Ryans -- not Jimmy Ryans, no, no.
Back in New York?

Back in New York. And I did a few record dates for the various singers and performers and a few concerts and as I said before, my wife is of Puerto Rican extraction and we began to think very strongly about returning to Puerto Rico. And in '65 I just bag and baggage -- put furniture on the boat and away to Puerto Rico we went.
How about your experiences in Puerto Rico?
Puerto Rico? I had ten years to learn Puerto Rico -- we stayed there for ten years before coming here.
Did you learn to speak the language?

Funny thing -- I didn't study the language in Puerto Rico. I tried to learn just enough words to get along and I got in the middle of something and don't you know, after about five years my English -- I couldn't -- had no command of vocabulary at all. I just couldn't think of words to say. Because on television I never understood -- because I
didn't take time to try to understand. So anybody would talk with me, after about eight or nine years, I didn't know what they were saying.
In English?

No, Spanish. In Spanish -- I wouldn't understand them. So, there wasn't enough English spoken to me daily for me to practice English, so after about eight years I couldn't speak English and I couldn't speak Spanish. As my wife will tell you, when I came here, she'd have to translate for me -- English, on television. Because I got in the habit of not listening, following conversations. I couldn't follow words -- I couldn't follow -- I didn't know what you were talking about anyhow, so I didn't follow the conversation. Television or in person. They're speaking in Spanish -[jibberish] and I'm looking out the window because I don't know what they're talking about anyhow. And -- but I didn't have sufficient opportunity to speak English so my English just slipped away -- believe it or not, and I couldn't speak Spanish and I couldn't speak English and I was in a heck of a fix.
How did work turn out for you there?

Well, I went to Puerto Rico -- I called a friend of mine from New York and asked him what the situation was down there and he said, 'Well, in the national band -- the state band, they'd like to have a bassoon player.' I said, 'Okay, I'm coming down.' So, we arrived in Puerto Rico on a

Sunday night and by Tuesday night I was working with the National Orchestra -- National Band, playing bassoon. They didn't have a decent bassoon player on the Island at that time. But the gimmick was, it only paid $200.00 a month. Mind you, $200.00 a month. But we had some aid. I stayed with my sister-in-law and her husband is one of the important horse trainers there and they had a big house, so they kept the four of us until I got on my feet. So I just turned over my -- when it got to me it was $190.00 a month and I just turned it over to my sister and gave her $130.00 a month and she fed us and took care until I got a break. Finally, I went from there to -- from the State Band -- I left and I joined the Puerto Rican Symphony. Oh, there was an increase of salary, about $116.00 a week -- a week. Oh, I was rich then. And I stayed with the symphony a season and a half and one day I was in a cleaning establishment and I met one of the conductors at one of the hotels, and he asked me if I'd like to join him. He heard that I was in town. I said, 'Yeah, I'd be glad to.' So, he gave me a job at the Americano with Ralph Font's orchestra and that was an increase to about $140.00 or something like that. And I stayed a couple years at the Americana and I left there and went to the San Juan Hotel -- they needed a piccolo player. When I arrived in Puerto Rico there weren't many guys who could double. They either played the saxophone or clarinet or trumpet. But a piccolo player or bassoon player or good

oboe player they didn't have. So, whenever an act came there that they needed a piccolo or oboe or bassoon, why I would go to the various hotels. So I did that for another couple years or so. And I met a trumbone player who was a jazz man from L.A., but he was making his living down there selling encyclopedias. Got rich. And also was a good jazz man. He couldn't read music but he could play. Very big guy -- Bob Smiten. So he introduced me to another fellow who I found out later on was president of Williams International which was the largest printing company in Puerto Rico, and he was also a frustrated pianist. So, he suggested why don't don't we organize a group and play, you know, get together for kicks and may be we can book something and keep going. Well, his wife was also a drummer. She wanted to be a drummer. She used to be a ballerina at the Roxy Theater before she married Williams in New York, and they'd been living in Puerto Rico for, then, when I first arrived, they'd been living there for 20 years. They had a large family and all. So, we organized this group with his wife playing drums and him playing piano, and we picked up a trumpet player, an old retired Army man from Texas playing trumbone, and we got this jazz band. And we played service clubs -- we played for the Navy, we played for the Air Force, and this Bill Williams, he wouldn't take any money and neither would his wife, so if the gig paid, say, $40.00 a piece, they gave me their $80.00 and with my $40.00 I had $120.00 for a gig.

And sometimes I'd make $150.00 a gig for myself. So, to me it was a good business. And I took on a few pupils too. Private teaching wasn't much because Puerto Ricans weren't in the habit of paying $10.00 a lesson or something.. They could go to the conservatory for a whole season for -- whole semester for $25.00 -- all year. Attend the conservatory -- $25.00. That's all it cost. Government subsidizes the rest of it, I think, through the Ford Foundation and some other benevolent society. And we kept on with this thing until Bill said, "I got another idea." Down in the candata -- that's down there where the Americans are, down the strip, "Why don't we get a cabaret?" I said, "Well, you can get a cabaret, I don't have --" He said, "Don't worry about that, I'll get a place." Well, that man had so much confidence in me and enjoyed it so much, he went out and bought a cabaret -- leased it, rather, and put $5,000.00 in my hands and said, "Now, here's your expense account, now put your band in." So, I got some other musicians and I replaced them with a drummer -- had a good drummer there, and also a piano player, Gene Gilbo, who was piano player with the Trainiers, from California. Most of them were stationed here. He'd been with them for 25 years. He joined me and we went into a club and we renamed it -- I've forgotten the name now, and we did three nights a week and I paid the guys a salary just the same, I had to dig in my pocket every week and pay because it -- Puerto Ricans hadn't really accepted jazz and the few Americans that

were there -- we were struggling hard to get them to come out. The weekends they would show up, but -- the owners of the club had the drinks and I got a percentage of the money -- 40 percent or something like -- 60 percent -- I got 60 percent. I'd still have to go to my pocket to help make the payroll every week. So, we stayed there long enough for somebody to hear about us. That somebody was Eastern Airlines and when the vice presidents had heard us and when they opened up their big hotel, the Saramar Beach, they had considered us -- I'd been out there to see them -- they decided on a Latin band for their opening attraction. After the first night they realized what a mistake they'd made, so they had to keep them six months. One thing about Puerto Rico, you have to -- you can't hire a man for two weeks and fire him. You keep him for the duration -- you either hire him for six months or the duration of the show, or, you know, like that. You can't hire him and then give him two weeks notice and fire him any time you want.
That's the law?

They had to keep them there six months. So, I hung on til my $5,000.00 was gone and by that time they were ready to take me on at Saramar. So we went out there more or less on trial. They said, well, if you can play a good show, you've got the job! So, I went out there for two weeks -- I stayed four years. Four years.
Did you keep the same band?

Well, I have made one or two changes, one or two changes, but basically I had the same bass player, I had the pianist -- Gene quit and then he came back. Gene was with me off and on three different times. He'd quit and come back, quit and come back. In the mean time I had one of the best Puerto Rican piano players, Lucito Ben Hamin, one of the greatest pianists on the Island. But he played too much piano for a band, he was all over the band, but a wonderful musician.
Did you -- were you playing mostly -- you said shows --
We played shows and dance music.
And dance music.
And the supper club with the Saramar Beach Hotel.
What were the shows?
Well, we brought in the acts -- we had stage like the --
Like a lounge show?

Yeah, collector's items, different acts, different attractions that came on, different singers. We had a fellow here from Phoenix, Arizona, who was a bar tender, but he got together a good act, comedy. He could imitate anybody, and it was through him -- he recommended us, said we played his music better than anybody ever played it, so the management was

convinced we were good for the room. And, as I say -- then they gave me a house -- big house right on the estate. It belonged to Rockefeller, you know -- that's who it actually belonged to. And I had one of Rockefeller's houses, a big two-story mansion there. And my back yard was right on the golf course, and I could go out and practice golf every morning. Go out on the beach right down -- and my dogs had the run of the whole neighborhood and the woods. It was just beautiful there, beautiful life in Puerto Rico.
But after ten years --

After ten years I wanted to come home, you know, you come home to your roots and it's -- I don't care how good things are. I left a good salary there -- a tremendous salary that I was getting, and I left it -- band, salary and just moved everything, all my furniture and brought it here. Just walked out on the job, but you see, one of the main reasons I left too, I was going blind. I have cataracts, and I was about 80 percent blind. I got so I couldn't --
In both eyes?

Both eyes, yes. Both eyes. And I had to wear black glasses to keep the light out so I could see a little bit, but it got so I couldn't go out at night and I could hardly see in the day, so, I decided to have an operation. My brother-in-law is training one of the horses -- some of the horses of the best ophthalmologist in Puerto Rico and we set up

a date for me -- he examined me, "Yes, you have cataracts, we'll have to take them out." So, he set up the date for the operation and I had the bed at the hospital, and the day of the operation, they were to operate on my eyes, and I came that morning and they gave me my injections and the fluid and the stuff I'm supposed to drink to put me in sort of semi-twilight sleep, supposed to be, and they put me in this gown and put me on the operating table and took me to the operating room.

I had my arms strapped and my legs strapped to the table, and I asked them why they had to strap me down. "Oh, yes, we have to prepare you, you know, you can't move an arm or leg or it would be disastrous." So, I said, "Okay." And I layed there for about 15, 20 minutes and I said, "Will you take these straps off me?" "No, no, we can't." So, I layed there for an hour in this cold operating room with just that gown over me and I'm freezing, and they got me strapped down. I begin to holler, "Take these damn things off my legs and arms," and I started raising -- so they unbuckled it. When they did that I got up off the operating table in a half stupor -- I was groggy, walked to the elevator in my short nightgown and got an elevator and went upstairs and my wife was in there and said, "What happened?" I said, "uh-huh." She said, "Oh, Garvin, you can't." I said, "I did it." She said, "You can't do that." I said, "I did it. I'll never let them butcher me up." Put my clothes on and drive 30 miles back to Durado in that half stupor

because she didn't have a license in those days. So, while I was dressing the doctor said, "What happened?" I said, "I got a little nervous, I got excited." He said, "Well, some other time?" "Yeah, some other time." And I knew then I was going to leave Puerto Rico because I was blind and I wanted that operation done in the States, but I didn't know where to go. I didn't know what doctor. I wasn't going to New York, I didn't figure Chicago, and I knew it would be a six-month layoff,-- six or seven months before I could do anything. So we picked Vegas. Now, we got here -- I took my kids to school the second day and I got lost. I couldn't read the street signs.
Could I back up a little here, because I recall speaking to your wife and she said that you actually drove from Miami to Las Vegas.

Oh, I did. Now, here's what happened. I was tricked. At the hospital, they had given me -- put drops in some sort of solution in my eyes that temporarily cleared them up and they stayed clear for about a week. And I said, "Well, I've got it made, my eyes are going to clear up." And it lasted until we got on the -- took a plane from Puerto Rico to Miami, we changed to Jacksonville. That day my eyes went back to the state of cataracts again - - went black, just blacked out. I'm in Jacksonville, the car's on the boat, I've got to drive it. There's nothing else for me to do but drive it. I couldn't see 20 feet ahead of me. I drove all the way across those
mountains in that condition.
With your family in the car?

Yes, my family and my dog and all in the car. I had to, there was nothing else I could do. They read the signs for me, "Turn left, turn right." What route I'm on, and I rode it. More than 80 percent blind, and God had to be with me, he had to be. And we didn't get lost one time. Came direct -- because I'd been over this route before going to California -- Route 10, you know, all the way from Jacksonville, takesyou right to Los Angeles, but I had to turn off at Tuscon and go up through Arizona to Flagstaff and like that. And made it. Didn't even have a blow out.
Amazing.

When it would rain or the sun got too bright on the highway, I'd have to stop. If the road had white dust on it, the reflection was too great, I couldn't see. It was just a vast cloud in front of me. And, as I say, when I got here, I couldn't find my way back. I got the kids to school, but -- he helped me to see the streets, but when I put him in school and came home, I got lost, and we didn't have the phone in yet and I couldn't call up Lu to come get me. She didn't know where to find -- you know, we were strangers. We didn't know anybody. I had to call up the real estate agent to find out what school to put my kid in, "Where do we put him? What school does he go to? What neighborhood? What Board of

Education?" All that -- the real estate agent helped me. So I knew then I had to have the operation and I had it on September 28. We arrived here September the 6th or 7th and I had this operation and that's it. And I couldn't even blow an instrument for six months because any pressure would have burst the small capillaries or something in my eyes. The operation would have been bad.
But the operation -- you've had it and it was successful?
I've had it now, yes, it's successful.
And you're looking forward to getting back on the stage.
Oh, I'm going back now full force. I came here to work, not to retire.
That's beautiful.

Yeah. And as I told you, I'm still looking forward to becoming one of the greatest oboe players in the world. I think I'm going to be the best oboe player in Las Vegas and I'm going other places to prove to them I'm one of the best oboe players in the country. And I still play at jazz, I still love jazz, it's my beginning. I still play jazz, I love it.
That's just fantastic. Now, we've started the conversation and arrived right up to date, but as you remember, we mentioned about going back over the yearsand
tap up on some areas we may have overlooked while coming along.
Yes, I think -- I look here -- looking over a list of things here, I think we should talk a little about one of the greats of jazz and my association with him, Bunk Johnson.
Right. I would like to hear about some of your experiences with him.

Yes, Bunk -- he sent for me to play in his band. Something happened to his clarinet player when he came to New York -- down to play in a concert with him down at Stuyvesant Casino, that's down on 2nd Avenue, I think.
Now, what year was this about?

This must have been '46, yeah. And I played this concert with him and he liked the way I played clarinet and I played another date with him, and he decided he had this album to make and he wanted me to play that album with him. He used all New York musicians -- Don Kirkpatrick on piano was a New Yorker, and he also used Ed Cuffy who was a trumbone player, he was in New York -- Cuffy was from the mid-west but he lived in New York for many years. He had on bass -- he had Pop Foster on bass, and drums -- who was on drums. He had a good drummer, I forgot who was on drums. But it was an all New York band. And this date he had, w e did it in 1947, was the day of the big snow in New York, the 1947 snow, the biggest snow they'd had since the blizzard of '88. We went into

Carnegie Hall. We recorded it in Carnegie Hall and we went into Carnegie Hall at 12:00 o'clock -- oh, (Well upon) Wilman Braud was the base player, not Pop Foster, Broe. William Braud, that's the name -- he's from New Orleans. And we went in at 12:00 o'clock and it just began to snow. When we came out at 5:00 that evening the busses were straddling the roads. There was snow, I think, three feet deep. That's how hard it had snowed in New York while we were recording. I remember Bunk saying -- he'd never seen snow, you know. He had never seen snow.
First time he'd seen snow?

Yeah. And he said, 'My God, look at all this stuff.' He picked it up and tasted it, and I never saw Bunk after that because he went back to New Orleans shortly after that. But Bunk, to my mind, he wasn't one of the -- wasn't the trumpet player that Louis was or Freddy Keppard, or Joe Oliver, or Dewey Jackson, but he may be a creator -- they played so much more than he played. I'll tell you what I'll do, I have an album here, one of the albums I made with him, I think we should play his interpretation of a tune was recently very popular, 'The Entertainer'. Now, we did this 30 years ago.
Okay. We'll pause here and play a track from that particular album.
(music)
Monk, that arrangement we played was not extemporaneous. We played right from the parts of the original

arrangement that was made about 1916 or 1917, so it gave it really the authentic sound of just how 'The Entertainer' was played many, many years ago. Most of the numbers that we did on this album Bunk had parts to them, you know, and we adhered right to the part and we played a few solos, but that's the way he wanted it. Monk -- Bunk - they're close. Bunk played, and I don't know how he did it, because he had false teeth, you know, he had upper and lower plates.
Both upper and lowers?

Upper and lower, and I don't how he played because when he'd get tired he'd take out both plates and rest his gums. But you can see he had been quite a figure to reckon with in playing trumpet. I heard a lot of the things -- either he played them first or Louis played them first -- I don't know. He got them from Louis or Louis got them from him, and I heard some of the old things King Oliver played. Bunk, I think, was probably older than -- he may have been the same age as King Oliver. Speaking of King Oliver leads me up to the impact that King Oliver had on Bubba Miley and myself when we first went to Chicago. We used to go to the dreamland every night and sit there with our mouths open listening to King Oliver play that horn.
What year was this?
This was 1921, we went out there with Mamie Smith. After we left the Persian Theater -- that incident

I told you some time back. We went to the Avenue Theater in Chicago. And every night Bubber and I would go to the Dreamland to hear King Oliver play. Bubber had never heard anything like that -- I'd heard some of it, but not as much, you know, sit there three and four hours at night. King Oliver was just the king of plain New Orleans jazz. He played with a tin mute in his mouth -- in his horn, and he got a growling effect. That's where Bubber Miley got the growl that he introduced to Duke Ellington.
Oh, I see. Then King Oliver was obviously the first.

That came from -- now Bubber was playing with Mamie Smith like Johnny Dunn with the plunger doing the wawa -- wa wa wa wa -- but King Oliver had a growl with the mute that came with cornet. In those days they didn't play trumpets, they played cornets. All the New Orleans boys played cornets. The easterners played trumpets. And Bubber got that growl, because every night after we finished up the show we would go to the Dreamland and sit there and listen to Johnny Dodds and Baby Dodds and King Oliver. Louis wasn't with him then, but Lil Armstrong and Dutrey was in the band. And that's where Bubber got his inspiration for playing -- he came back to New York and finally he joined Duke, and with Charlie Ervis having done the wa wa with a growl on trombone with Duke's band, that's where the origin -- funny thing -- Duke's style was

created in New York by New York musicians. Bubber was a New Yorker and so was Charlie Ervin, and those were the two guys that put the growl in Duke's band that gave him his style. Two New Yorkers, not southerners or westerners, they were New Yorkers. Two New York born boys. Bubber was born down in Hell's Kitchen and I think Charlie Ervis was born not too far from there. Both New Yorkers, and Duke's style came from a New York style of playing -- the growl. You see, the growl was developed, you know, King Oliver created it, but they were New Yorkers that did it, emulating what they heard in the west and they turned around and made a style for Duke Ellington. So Duke wrote from then on. He wrote everything -- East St. Louis Toalle-o-o (unintelligible) and that growl and the minor thing, that's where it came.
Is that right?

Yes, yes. And, Bubber was the main stay. He created the style for that band, he and Charlie Ervis. While I'm on the subject of the origin of Duke's style, I would also like to mention the type of bands that were in New York in those days in the very early '20's, the dance halls -- you had bands of 30 and 40 and 50 pieces, and they were composed of banjos, bandeleens, violins, trumpets, trumbones, maybe one or two saxiphones. Saxophone hadn't been quite popular then. The bandoleen was half violin and half banjo, made by Felon Harlen, you picked it like you did a banjo, but it had a violin neck and
a head like a banjo, called a bandoleen.
Right.
And they'd have 40 and 50 of those sometimes the orchestras were conducted by John C. Smith or Allie Ross or Happy Roan, at the New Star Casino. When you went to dance you heard 40 and 50 musicians.
And they were like -- this was like an average band?
An average big dance band, New Star Casino or Manhattan Casino or Rockland Palace, which is now Rockland Palace.
And there was quite a few would be working at one time, right in New York?

Well, they'd have the big dance, and they couldn't afford more than one going at a time -- it wouldn't be the same night, but for a dance, not worked nightly on the roof and the Ziegfield Roof and those places, maybe there was 15 pieces. When they were over at the __________ they had about 12 pieces. But when you played like New Star Casino or Manhattan Casino, then they had 40 or 50 pieces in the dance band. And I only saw that in New York, but it was quite a thing to listen to.
Now, Mr. Bushell, can you tell me a little bit about your first broadcast.
Hó, ho, this has to be one of the first
I made it the way we did it. Well, it was with Sam Wooding's band. We were having a rehearsal at the Nist one afternoon --
What year was this?
Okay.

And one of the guys said, "We should -- as good as this sounds we should be broadcasting somewhere." Radio was just coming into its own then. "Broadcast, how are you going to -- this place doesn't have broadcasts." The drummer said, "Let's go to the studio then." "Come on, stop joking." He said, "Yeah." So Sam said, "He's got something there. Let's do it." I said, "Okay, let's pack up." We packed up the band, bag and baggage and put them in two taxi cabs -- this was way up in Harlem, and went all the way down to the Bell Telephone Company which is down at Wall and Broad, lower Manhattan.
Yeah, right.

And we left the band in the cabs at the curb and Sam and I walked into this station which was then WJZ owned by the Bell Telephone Company. And a lady said, "May I help you?" "We'd like to see the fellow in charge of broadcasting?" This fellow come out and said, "Can I help you?" We said, "Yes, we have a band out there we'd like for you to hear." So he looked at the other fellow and kind of smiled and one of those things -- tongue in cheek, and said, "You have a band
outside?" And we said, "Yes, we've got a band outside." It took nerve, you know, we're standing there shivering.
This was your idea, right?

Yeah. So, he said, "You have a band outside?" We said, "Yeah." He said, "Well, bring them in." They're still looking at each other and laughing, so I went out and said, "Come on, fellows," and they said, "You sure?" I said, "Yeah, come on, they want us in there." And we brought them in and just stood there and the guys with the horns and the drums and the bass -- and what do we do next. The fellow say, "Well, set up. Come on in the studio and set up in the studio." And set up and still frightened, but we were fighters, you know. We knew we had something good and we didn't get so nervous that we couldn't play. We kept our composure.
But I would think they were looking forward to a big laugh.

They were looking for a big laugh, you know. They hadn't heard of us, there was no black band on radio then, outside of Fletcher Henderson, that was a big name jazz band, see. Fletcher had gone -- no, no, he hadn't gone, he was still at Club Alabam. There was no broadcasting -- there was no black band on radio at all, there was none. So, we set up, tuned up, and the fellow said, "All right, begin when you want to." And we started playing one of our best numbers. Before we'd finished the middle of the arrangement, they rang

the buzzer and we said, 'Oh, my God, we blew that. That's gone. They're going to throw us out.' The guy came in and said, 'You guys, would you like to go on the air?' 'Why, certainly,' Sam says. 'Well, the Army band -- the United States Army Band has been canceled, you can do a coast-to-coast at 4:00 o'clock, one half hour -- can you do a half-hour broadcast?' 'Oh, we can do two hours.' And they put us on the air coast-to-coast in place of the United States Army Band and that was the beginning of Sam Wooding's band developing to being a great organization.
Is that right?
Just through sheer nerve and determination that we had something to sell.
They put you on that day?

They put us on that day, right then and there, and it so happened that something happened and the Army band had to cancel it's 4:00 o'clock spot. I guess the President or somebody had sent for them to go some place else, and we filled the place. It was substitute for the United States Army Band, coast-to-coast radio.
After you made that one day --

Well, we naturally went back to the Nist but so many people heard us and we got letters and we did vaudeville. Then we went into vaudeville around -- in and around New York, not too far so we could come back and make our engagement at the Nist every night. But this agent had heard
about the band, Arthur Lyons, and that's how we happened to get the European engagement.
Is that right?
Yes, he planned the whole thing and then we went to Europe.
That was in 1923 we did that and it took us up to '25 before we hit the top. It was two years, but we made it.
Mr. Bushell, can you recall any memorable incidents that happened when you were traveling with Wooding?

Well, there were many. It's been 50 years -- 55 years ago and it's pretty hard for me to recall all of them. But I do remember a particular incident that happened while playing for an afternoon party for the queen of Spain. You know, she was English, she was married to King Alfonso, but she was English, very attractive, buxom blond, and we had been chosen to play this afternoon tea. There were a lot of British royalty there and Spanish royalty and dignitaries at this afternoon tea party. And we're playing -- let me sort of set -- give you the situation. We had a saxophone player and a trombone player who had bad blood for each other. It was either through envy or jealousy or just plain dislike for each other, I don't know which, but they

never got along. And this particular time the trombone player was standing up playing a solo and the saxophone player began to noodle in his solo and distract him. And they'd had this problem before, so the trombone player put his trombone down and walked over and squared off at the saxophone player. Well, we all jumped up to grab him so naturally the band stopped and the queen got up and put her to her eyes and she said, "My, my, what is going on?" And Sam -- we're all trying to separate these two guys in this beautiful parlor of the palace of the King of Spain -- these two American musicians wanted to fight about who was to play a solo. And Sam said, "When I get you outside, I'm going to kill both of you." And it took all of us to keep Sam off of them when we got outside. Oh, Sam would have killed them both. They're both dead now. Willie Lewis and Herb Flemming. Flemming just died this past year.
But they did finish the engagement out for the Queen?

Well, after we cooled down we played a couple more tunes and the charge of the palace said, "That will be all Mr. Wooding," to get us out of there. Did you know a singer named Robson that used to be with Claude Hopkins orchestra?
No.
I had -- that happened to me on a gig in

New York once. I used to play for the rich people in New York in the '30's, you know, and I was playing for the Vanderbilts and I had to go out and play at parties for them. I used to take Fats out with me to Vanderbilt's house all the time.
Oh, (unintelligible)

He always told me, "Bring that fat one, the one that plays that organ." Vanderbilt would invite us out to his house just by -- nobody there, no party -- he'd say, "Garvin, what are you doing today?" "Nothing." "Can you bring four or five guys out -- and bring that fat one?" "All right." "Come on out to the house." "When do you want us?" "Soon as you can get here." I'd get the guys together and I'd get Fats and a drummer and myself and we'd go out to his house. He'd be there by himself, W. K. Vanderbilt, and we'd sit up and play a couple tunes and he'd sit there listening, tapping his feet. "Okay, let's talk a while." And he liked to talk about Europe. He liked to talk about Russia, because being a Vanderbilt they wouldn't allow him -- he was a Capitalist, and they wouldn't allow him in Russia in those days, in the '30's. He'd say, "Garvin, How's -- do they do -- what's so and so -- what do they do there, so and so?" And we'd eat and drink and play another couple of tunes and he'd reach in his pocket -- if he had $500.00 or $300.00, he'd give it to me right out of his pocket and say, "Hey, here you are, give it to the boys, divide it with the boys." And he was a very unhappy man. I think he

died, they said, of a broken heart. He used -- very often he'd say to us, "I have you boys out here because you're genuine and if I could have just half the fun that you guys have, but I can't because everybody B.S.'s me. I don't who's genuine, who means what they say in my own family." He was the most miserable man -- then he had over $300 million. So, Fats used to say, "Mr. Vanderbilt, you give me some of your money, I'll show you how to have fun." And that would knock him out. That would kill him.
Well, Fats was really known to be a very humorous man.

Oh, he was a big child. Now, getting back to Spain -- this Queen, she had a habit of coming to our theater after the opening -- after the opening would start, you know, and we'd be right in the middle of our big opening, the girls are dancing, the band's playing, the cymbal's flying, and she'd walk in -- well, the minute she makes her entrance into her box, everything must stop. You stop, the girl's got her leg up, you stop right there. And you stop and play the Spanish National Anthem and then she and everybody sits down. Then you proceed and pick up whereyou left off. And she did that -- we were in Madrid about six weeks and she at least came once a week and every time she came we'd have to stop -- she came in almost near the ending of the opening and we'd have to stop it. Sometimes we'd have to do it over. Somebody would say, "Do it

from the beginning." And that to us was a very big joke. You know, in Spain they had the claque. If you owned a theater and I own a theater, you have a big attraction at your theater, I'll send a group of 15 or 20 to go in your theater and every act that comes on they'll boo -- they'll boo everything that comes on. I'd pay them to do that -- they call that the claque. And we thought that was the funniest thing we ever saw in -- heard in our lives. Having to stop in the middle of the show to play the National Anthem -- so we had a great time in Spain.
And I also remember one night after our performance they had bouts -- boxing bouts.
Prize fights.
Prize fights, yeah.
Professional?

Yeah, professional, yeah. And I think Paulino -- I saw Paulino there, Paulino Scodoon. He was on one of the cards. Anyhow, one of the boxers didn't show up, so they said, 'We're one bout short.' So we had a Russian dancer, a little guy named George State, and he was a feather weight. He had done some pro boxing but he wasn't good enough, so he went back to doing dancing, Russian dancing -- knee drops and all that sort of thing. So, they said, 'We're short a bout.' So George said, 'I'll fight him.' 'Come on, George, the man will kill you, he's in training.' 'I'll fight him.' And it turned out this bout was the feather weight champion, because the main bout

was a middle weight and a heavy weight bout. This feather weight champion was supposed to box an exhibition bout with somebody and the guy didn't show up, I guess he got cold feet. George said, "I'll fight him."
George hadn't been in training?

No, he hadn't trained or anything. No, he was dancing everyday, that's the only thing. Doing his knee drops and -- so the boy said -- George said, "Don't hit me hard because I just finished eating because I didn't think I was going to fight." Then in Spanish, they had an interpreter, "I won't hit you hard." George went in there and boxed around, careless, and the boy hit George and knocked George down. Instead of George falling, he did a flip back -- he was a tumbler, too, you know. He did a back flip and come up fighting. Well, the Spaniards went wild. George -- in the first round George knocked him out cold. The feather weight champion and George knocked him out cold in the first round. A buck dancer so to speak. And those were some of my experiences in Spain besides seeing the bull fights and all. I'd turn my head every time the horses hit the bulls, so I didn't go any more to that. Spain was a great place.
Mr. Bushell, can you think of any more memorable incidents?
Right -- as they say -- off the top of my head I can remember an incident in Copenhagen. We left the
show in Copenhagen and the show went on back to Germany, but we stayed there a while, trying to settle our affairs and deciding what we were going to do.
What year if you recall?

1925. I think it was around October -- something like that -- September, because I had my birthday there. And one of the young ladies whom I'd met at one of the cabarets, sent me a big bouquet to my hotel and I wasn't there, but when I got through this bouquet was strewn all over the floor. My wife had received them and tore this bouquet into shreds. And speaking of the women of Denmark, they just took us off our feet. They thought we were the greatest things they'd ever seen. And they're beautiful women, too, the Danish women. Very feminine, extremely feminine. And we would go to the cabarets -- I remember this club called the Alure Club, and instead of the hostesses entertaining the millionaires and the rich men, they'd come over to us. And they weren't doing their job, so the management said, 'Look, I'm glad to have you here, but the girls aren't doing their job, so would you please stay out of my cabaret?' And he actually forbid us to come to the -- 'No, the girls will not work.' And they just went wild about these American musicians.
But there was never any violence really --
No violence, just great fun. I'm telling

you, this lady that went head over heels about me and she sat down in my hotel lobby and my wife's upstairs. Let me tell you more about this Denmark thing. We left the show and I had been buying dogs and diamond rings and naturally when we left the show I was broke. So I had my wife with me and two Great Danes. You know how big Great Danes are. Well, I ran out of money and naturally I couldn't buy food for my Danes. But in Europe, there's a custom that when you have your meals served in your room, you put your plates outside of the door and they pick them up. And this hotel we stayed in -- just a few years ago it burned to the ground, and 23 Americans were burned in that hotel, I remember. Anyhow, I had one can of string beans between my wife and two Great Danes. And I had a seven Kronen bill and I went to the telegraph office to send a cable to my father to send me money -- seven Kronen wouldn't even start it. So, I said, 'Lord, what am I gonna do?' I'm too proud to ask Wooding and let him know that I'm broke, you know, while I'm strutting with my cane all the time. And, so we got hungry and I didn't have any food, so I got a paper bag at a grocery store and I went -- there were about six floors in this hotel and I went to every floor and got scraps out of these plates and cleaned the plates out to fill the bag to feed my dogs.
