My wife and I still had nothing but this can of string beans. So we ate a little of it for breakfast -- cold string beans -- we ate a little for dinner. I said, 'I can't hold out any longer.'

So we had a rehearsal that afternoon. I was -- this was the third day. And we had rehearsal and I couldn't blow. Sam said, "What's wrong with you?" "I don't feel good." He looked at me and said, "You don't look good, what's wrong with you? Are you sick?" "Yeah, I don't feel good in my stomach." So he says, "Drink some water. What's the matter with you, Garvin?" "Sam, I'm hungry." "What?" Sam was almost like a brother. "You're hungry? And you didn't tell me?" "Well, I don't tell you everything." He said, "Rehearsal's off, we'll rehearse tomorrow." And Sam put $10.00 -- the equivalent of $10.00 in Kronen in my hand and I went down to the hotel and got my wife and we went down to the dining room and ate up all the $10.00, I think, the first meal. Anyhow, we couldn't make our connections and we communicated with the owners of the show -- they were in Hanover. So we told them we'd rejoin the show in Hanover. We were going to quit because something happened to Sam and his business -- some royalty he was supposed to have gotten and they didn't give it to him -- but we didn't quit. We went back with the show, rejoined them in Hanover and everybody was glad to see us because there was 53 people stranded and here's a band of 12 men, and I was glad to get back with the show because I didn't have a quarter. I remember distinctly I landed in Germany with my wife and this trunk full or horns and I had a quarter. When I landed in Hamburg after working the Club Alabam -- money -- as fast as I got it I spent it.

You know, you don't hold on to money because you knew you were going to work all the time. So I bought clothes and I bought automobiles, and when I landed in Germany, I had one 25 cents. So, we gotready to move in Hamburg to get dinner before we got on the train for Berlin -- I sat in the corner with my wife and Sam said (unintelligible) long time -- five hours." "I ain't got no money, Sam." He said, "What? Are you broke again?" Oh, Sam, I loved him. As I told you, he's still living, though. He's 82 years old and still going.
He was obviously a great guy to work for.

Oh, he was a great guy, great guy. I love him, love him. He's like my father -- he taught me so much coming up. He's a little older than I am -- as I say, he's 82. And we finally left Denmark -- but I'm telling you, I've since then wanted to back to Denmark. I know a lot of guys go to Denmark and stay. What's the cello player -- the bass player that went there and stayed? Cello player -- Ben Webster went there and stayed. A lot of guys go there and stay and just live because Denmark is just one of the finest countries in Europe. And the women are so much woman, you know. You've never seen anything like it. Yes, yes.
Now, you've told us about some of the happy experiences during your tour in Europe. Did you ever run into any more unfortunate experiences while in Europe?

I remember distinctly the opening night after the show -- the opening performance in Berlin in Admiral's Palace -- that was on Frederickstrasse -- there were people out front crowded around the performers and musicians and we were receiving the congratulations from the public who had seen our first show -- how great -- they loved the music and all --
What year was this, Mr. Bushell?

1925, May 3 or 6th, something like that. And everybody was commenting and saying how well we performed, how much they loved our work, and saying what a great show it was. But one German evidently had too many drinks and he came right up into the crowd and tore open his shirt and said, 'I'm a German to my heart. I don't understand why the government allows these black people to come to our country. During the war they cut off our noses, they cut off our ears,' he's speaking about the Senegalese, you know. The Senegalese didn't take prisoners, they just -- when a German went down they just cut off the end of his nose or an ear and put it on a string. That way when he went back home that shows how many men he captured -- killed rather. He said, 'They did that to us and I have not forgotten. And I am not going to stand for it. They should run them out of Germany.'
Was he speaking in German?
He was speaking in German. I understand, I studied German from a kid -- my grandfather was German, so I

studied German in school. And he turned around to one of the dancers, Rufus Green to be exact, and grabbed Green by the coat. When he grabbed Green he clipped him on the chin and down he went. Now, he was so drunk he couldn't stand up. When Green hit him he went down and got up and shook himself and walked just as straight down Frederickstrasse as you've ever seen anybody right out of the crowd. That straightened him out. We found out in those days, you know, the Germans used to carry large canes. And a German is funny. If he hollers at you and you wilt, he'll beat you to death. But if he hollers at you and you holler back and get up in his face, he's ready to go. We found that out. We found the weak spot. I'll tell you what we found. We were sitting in a backroom in a place called the Domstatterhof one night. There were five of us in there having beer, and six or seven Heidelberg students came in. You could tell Heidelberg students because they were medical students and they all had scars on the left side of their face. They're from medical school, I think it was Heidelberg -- but they all had scars on the left side -- they were all dueling students, you know. Everybody's got a cut -- all the medical - old Germans have cuts on the side of their face from school. They locked the door saying, "Now, we're going to run the schwartzes out tonight. What are you doing in Germany?" We looked at them, and I answered them in German, "We're here playing in the show. We're entertaining." "Ve don't vant you

here. Why don't you get out?" "We don't have anything to do with that." So, they locked the door and Bobby Martin picked up his glass of beer to drink it and they dumped the glass of beer out of his hand. When they did that -- we had a fellow who was an ex-fighter, another dancer, Chick Horsey. George wasn't on the scene that night, he was out in the street somewhere. But Chick Horsey was even tougher than George. We had an English boy, a violinist named Boucher -- he weighed about 190, 6'2" -- there was Bobby Martin, myself and Herb Flemming. Well, when they knocked the beer out of Bobby's hand, we stood up and we started slugging. I just put my head down, man, but I got knocked down real quick. I didn't weigh but 140 pounds soaking wet then, so they knocked me down real fast. But those other four guys cleaned these students -- the students unlocked the door and got out. You know, they unlocked the door -- we didn't come out -- they unlocked the door to come out. And they had to carry them out. They laid them out, and Boucher got outside with his cane. He was born in England -- he was an English Negro, and as Chick Horsey would knock them and shove them out, Boucher would flatten them with the cane. And they had to carry them out. So, they threatened to bring the whole school back the next night, but they never showed up. That was one of the bad incidents of Berlin. We had another incident in Zurich, Switzerland. I'm always involved in these things. I don't know how I got mixed up -- always something

happened, I was there. Three of us, and we're sitting in a bar and a fellow sitting right on the other side of the room -- everytime he'd smoke a cigarette butt down, he'd flip it over at us -- flip it over at our table. So, Sam Wooding's a funny guy. If he tells you he's going to hit you or he's going to shoot you, or what he's going to do, he'll do it. So, Sam just casually said, "If he flips another one of those cigarettes over here, I'm going to throw this glass at him -- I'll throw this ashtray at him." I thought Sam was kidding. And sure enough, the next cigarette butt he flipped over hit Sam right here.
On the forehead.

Right on theforehead. The other butts that he flipped over hadn't hit anybody, but this one hit Sam. Sam drew back with the ashtray and -- as the guy flipped his cigarette he picked up his glass of beer and started drinking. Sam threw the ashtray and cut that glass of beer off right in his hand, cut it off in his hand. Well, the Swiss -- they still if you're a great marksman -- he showed what he could have done. He could have hit him in the head if he wanted to. Cut the glass of beer off right in his hand. Well, he just stood up -- the manager said, "Nobody's going to bother you now." And we just stood up, paid our check and walked out, and nobody bothered us. Didn't even follow us or nothing. It scared him to death.
He thought that was just a warning.

That was a warning of what he could do. Sam said, 'I'd never be able to do that again if my life --' Oh, man, if he could talk to you now he'd tell you about that. 'God must have been with me.' Because he aimed it at his head and he missed his head and hit the glass, but the glass of beer right off in his hand.
So they thought --
Ghost that wouldn't tell.
-- this is a warning.
Oh, yes.
Now, Mr. Bushell, you mentioned about working at Leroy's. Could you tell us a little bit more about your experiences at Leroy's?
Well, there were many --
This is back in the '20's, right?

Yes, that was in '21, I think. There were many things that happened at Leroy's but I do remember something that had an impact on the whole world. There was a fellow -- youngster -- young boy from Charleston, South Carolina, by the name of Russell Brown, and he didn't have any work but he could do the dance that they did in Charleston, South Carolina, called the cut out. And we put him on for him to do his dance every night and then people would throw money on the floor to him and that's how the youngster made a living. He was in New

York and trying to make it, and every night he'd come in and get his ration -- he'd go around to all the cabarets, so he was nicknamed Charleston, because he came from Charleston and everybody called him that. "Charleston, want to do your dance?" and they'd put him on. And he'd do this cut out. So eventually they'd say, "Do the Charleston, Charleston, do the Charleston." And the name of the dance originated in New York City because in Charleston itself it was called the cut out. But it became Charleston in New York City at Leroy's Cabaret by Russell Brown who created the -- who presented the dance in New York. But it was named after Russell Brown -- his nickname, which is Charleston.
Exactly where it came from?
Exactly where it came -- how the dance became the Charleston.
That's interesting.
Yeah. Oh, many things happened at Leroy's. That was, you know, the most unusual place in the world.
Mr. Bushell, I notice you've been making a few notes and before closing, maybe you can just expound on a few of the things there at random that you'd like to talk about.
I noticed that we were taking this -- trying to do this interview in chronological order, but I find
in doing so I've skipped some things -- forgotten some things -- I say, these things happened 50 years ago, 55 years ago.
Yeah.

Some of them 60 years ago. And some things maybe are worth while. One thing in particular -- during our South American tour I remember our opening day at the Variety Theater in Buenos Aires I had a solo to play -- a sax solo, an aria from La Boehme --
Could I ask you what year this was?

This was 1926. With the saxophone quartet -- we had a saxophone quartet and we were doing the aria from La Boehme, and I'm playing the lead sax and I'm supposed to make the first eight bars and I stepped out to the footlights and there's a big orchestra in the pit and they're all looking -- opening day of this great American band -- we'd just come from Europe then. We hadn't been back in the States inquite some time. And as I hit the lights, I forgot completely what I was supposed to do. I couldn't think of the first note I didn't know what -- my mind went absolutely blank. So Sam is hitting the arpeggios on the piano and giving me the lead note -- I don't hear a thing. I couldn't think and it frightened me so, when he did give me the note and when it came to me what I'm supposed to play, I had no breath, so the aria was this section --
(humming)
-- but here's the way I played it. It was supposed to be a beautiful thing.
(humming)

-- and the people screamed. They thought I was doing comedy, and the guys in the pit just fell out. And the papers the next day said, "The saxophone player did one of the most humorous take-offs on the aria of La Boehme you've ever heard. And it wasn't because I couldn't do it, but it frightened me so, I had no breath. And we finally got through it and the guys were laughing, the rest of the quartet was laughing. It was comedy, so we kept it that way.
It was in the act, right?

Right. Another thing I remember in Buenos Aires -- I stayed at a German hotel there and one of the acts stayed there that was playing at the other theater -- it was a snake act. The guy had big snakes he'd perform with, and I think one of his pythons must have gotten out of the cage, anyhow, the buildings are constructed in South America -- in Buenos Aires -- the hallway is on the outside of the building with a roof over it, but they're attached to the outside of the building. So I had to walk from front of my -- I had the front room -- back to the kitchen. My wife had called me to come and eat my dinner. And as I passed by a room, I hear "pssssss" and I look back and here's the head of this huge python sticking out the transom. WEll, if you want to make me

run into the river or jump off the Empire State Building, just give me a snake, or shake a snake at me -- I'm gone. Well, I backed up against the wall of this outside hall, I hit my head and knocked myself out.
You didn't realize you were backing up so fast.

I hit my head and knocked myself out. They say, when they picked me up the snake was about a foot from me. He had crawled out this transom and in the meantime they went to the theater and got the guy and he put the snake back in. They said I was mumbling something in a foreign tongue they never understood before that. They put water on me and carried me back to the room. I didn't see how far the snake got out, but they said the snake was almost -- he had come out at least four foot and was down over the transom and was coming down the door. He was an 18 foot python. A monster python. Buenos Aires at that time was inhabited by many Germans. There were at least 50,000 Germans, so I was right at home in Buenos Aires. I'd go to the beer halls and speak German and they'd say, 'Are you German?' 'Ja, ich bin ein Deutscher (unintelligible)' And I had a ball in Buenos Aires. I loved it, and especially playing beside the great tango orchestras and they're trying to play jazz and we were playing tango. Had a great time. I think at this time, I think we should mention -- I should come back to the States because there's a character I think -- he

passed on last year too, one of the greats. I've mentioned his name already in connection with Duke Ellington. He had the band that brought Duke Ellington to New York. I'm referring to Elmer Snowden again. This time I'd like to tell of my experience with Snowden when he had the band at the famous Hot Feet, owned by one of the toughest gangsters in New York --
Now, Hot Feet was a club?

Hot Feet Club, down in the Village. They had four waiters who were also a quartet and they had four girls who were singers -- eight entertainers and we had seven in our band. Snowden's band then consisted of four saxophones, banjo -- must have had eight -- four saxophones, banjo, piano, bass and drums. That was eight.
Was this -- are we back in the '20's now?
This was in '30, 1930.

And we were then splitting the money -- the money had to go eight -- 16 ways, and I was coming home with $10.00 and $15.00 a night, but you know who came to our Hot Feet Club? Boston Blackie made at least two visits a week -- the original Boston Blackie. He was -- had the most handsome teeth of anybody I've ever seen. And he always grinned. He'd paste $1,000.00 bills on each one of the waiter's heads and let them run around all night with $1,000.00 pasted on his
forehead, you know. He'd collect them up before he left.
Yeah.

But that was his fun. He'd give each waiter a $100.00 -- each singer a $100.00 bill and make her stick that in her stocking. And we'd have to keep an eye on the entertainers because they'd go south with the money -- they had to come back and put in the box, you know -- we'd split it up. And we -- instead of playing the music for the entertainers we always had a lookout. My turn to look out. You just pretend you're playing, but you watch every move. The next time Otto would look out, or Crawford Worthington, who was once the first alto with the Blue Rythm Band. And Bingie Madison. And we had a band -- we used to broadcast from Hot Feet.
Live?

Live. We had four saxophones -- we never used music. You see, in those days the musicians from that era had tremendous ears and they had the great sense of harmonic value. Everybody could play four-part harmony. Otto was the lead saxophone, I was second alto, Crawford was the third alto and Bingie -- three altos and one tenor. We played four-part harmony to everything without music, and we broadcast without music.
Is that right?
And it's too bad the band never recorded.

And we didn't have to rehearse a tune. We'd say, 'Well, let's play this tune.' Everybody knew it. I tell my boys -- my students -- you never learn a melody unless you learn the harmony at the same time, because if you don't know the harmony, you don't know the music. You don't know it. So, everybody was familiar with the harmony of everything we played. And it was just fantastic how we could play four-part -- not three-part -- four-part harmony. Bingie Madison was a very qualified arranger. He was a master of theory in harmony, and we went on the air with that and they said it was the greatest four saxophones they'd ever heard -- we didn't have any music. It was like Wilbur de Paris's band -- no music. Musicians could do that then -- they didn't -- and they could play -- it wasn't like playing one single solo, but I mean they could play parts. I can play for you some of the things I did with Wilbur de Paris -- five-part harmony -- four and five-part harmony -- no music. But that was part of the bag then, it was part of -- they weren't great readers, but they could play so well without music. And, so Snowden -- we asked for a raise, and Gene Tunney used to come there all the time and his brother -- he had a brother was almost the size of Gene, and let's see, all the gangsters from New York used to come in, and they'd all spend money. See who could outspend each other, and we'd go home with at least $15.00 or $20.00 a piece, splitting it 16 ways. We only made $30.00 a week salary -- $30.00 a week

salary, but I averaged -- and we worked seven nights a week, too, you see, and you had $130, $140, $150.00 a week. You could figure on that. And that was right during the depression. The depression started in '30, you know, because the crash was in '29, and that was in '30 when things were rough. Musicians were hungry. But we had that job -- so, something happened. Snowden- told him we wanted a raise. Said he wouldn't give it to us. So, we said, "Well, we quit." Snowden gave him his notice. So, it's time to quit, this gangster -- Harry Lyons said, "You better not take that band out of here." Snowden said, "What do you mean?" "You better not take them out of here. If you do, you'll find yourself in the gutter." Snowden said, "All right, you'll see." Snowden had already told us, "When I give you a signal, have your horns packed." I gave the signal -- we had our horns packed sitting on thestand. And when we finished that night, "You better not take these instruments out of here." So, Snowden said, "Well, we're going to take them out and we're going to quit." And we walked out of the place -- the guy threatened us, said, "Youse won't get up town. I'm going to dump you in the river before you get up town." Snowden said, "Well, start dumping." Snowden always had a pistol in his pocket. Snowden had more nerve than anybody I've ever seen. Had the guts of a mountain lion. The -- one of the greatest guys I know. We were like brothers. We even bought automobiles in partnership. We bought -- one night

we're sitting on the job -- I was his straw boss when we were playing at Small's Paradise. A guy came in, "Who's got the keys to that blue Chrysler out there?" "Who wants to know?" "Finance." Snowden said, "You got them, Garvin?" "No, I forgot them." He looked at me -- he knew I had the keys. Snowden says, "No, he don't have the keys." He said, "Well, I'm going to haul it, I'm going to take it away." And sure enough, they took our Chrysler away from us, right while we were on the job. We were making money -- the salary was $50.00 a week, but I made tips -- I used to lend money to him because I had a little bank roll I got from Hot Feet, you know. I used to lend waiters this money and charge 10 percent interest and all that. And, but we were -- I tell you I didn't start realizing that I had an obligation to try to save money until I was about 45, 50 year old. I was throwing it away and having a ball.
But unfortunately, that band was never recorded?

Never recorded. Snowden was a great banjo player, you know. He came from Baltimore and Washington where all the banjo players came from in those days. Great banjo players of the country came from Baltimore.
Did you do any arranging for that group?
Yes, I did for the shows and I did some of the arrangements we played at Smalls. We had -- Al Sears was with us. We had -- anybody that you might know now -- no,

I don't think anybody that you know now, but I did some of the arranging for the band in those days, too, as well as the Apollo Theater. That's about as much as I can elaborate on Snowden. I think it's worth mentioning about another one of our great leaders. I mentioned his name before. I've been connected with Fletcher from his time -- first arrival in New York up to the time he passed. But I remember -- Fletcher made a lot of mistakes as we all have, and they always say Fletcher died of frustration, and a lot of those things were of his own doing -- I know that. For example, you know, he was the chief arranger for Benny Goodman, and we were both scheduled to play at Savoy the same night, and every arrangement he made for Goodman he made a copy for himself for his band. But Goodman went on ahead of us -- we couldn't go on, because every number that we were going to play, Goodman had played ahead of us. And we couldn't go on. The people yelled, so they said, "Well, he's chicken. He's afraid to complete against Benny Goodman." And that hurt him worse than anything else. And there were more of his mistakes. Now, Chick Webb, before the advent of Ella Fitzgerald, the band wasn't in demand like it became later on. He owed us for so many gigs we'd done and he didn't pay, so finally out on Long Island one night we finished playing the dance -- there was no money, so we were passing a wooded area of Long Island and we just opened the car and put Chick and his drums and books right out on the

road. It's 4:00 o'clock in the morning. He said, "I don't care, I don't care." Put him out on the road with his drums, his books and everything, and ran off and left him. So, it was blowing up a storm, so the driver said, "I better go back and get him." You know, when we went back to get that rascal, he's sitting there in the pitch dark in the woods, he said, "I don't care, you didn't have to come." And he wasn't as big as a --
He was still there?
Sitting right there. "You didn't have to come back and get me."
The band put him out?
The band put him out. I was one of them that helped push him out. Oh, he was a great little guy, though.

You know, this has been a wonderful 50, 60, 62 years, I guess, and all the experiences I've had and the fun. I got some of my -- I was inspired and it was more gratifying for some of the things I did with Everett Lee and Dean Dixon, two of our greatest black symphony conductors. I played concerts with both of them. And coming to Las Vegas -- I came here not to retire. I came here with a new idea that I was going to go on, and I intend to go on. I intend to open up the situation here and I think it needs it. And I have -- a lot of my friends said, "You came to Vegas to retire?" "No, not at all." I came here to really stir it up. So, I'm going to play some good jazz and some good old bassoon in Las
Vegas, so I hope I'm successful.

Garvin, I'd like to just and a little to what you're saying now, and express myself and mention one thing in particular. What a pleasure it's been forme just to meet and to know you.
